t: What a pump does, and the two ways of doing it
b: Every pump spends energy to raise, move or pressurise a liquid. There are only two fundamentally different ways to achieve it, and the distinction governs almost everything else about the machine's behaviour. A positive displacement pump traps a fixed volume of liquid and pushes it out mechanically. Flow is set by geometry and speed, essentially independent of the pressure it is working against, so the machine will keep raising pressure until something gives. Positive displacement pumps are self-priming, handle high viscosity well, and need relief protection on the discharge. A roto-dynamic pump — the centrifugal family — adds velocity energy to the liquid with a rotating impeller, then converts that velocity into pressure in a stationary collector. Because the energy transfer depends on the velocity triangles at the impeller, flow and head are coupled: increase the head the pump works against and flow falls away on its own. That self-regulating characteristic is why a centrifugal pump can be safely throttled and why it dominates process plant. Why this matters in practice A centrifugal pump cannot generate more than its shut-off head, so a closed discharge valve produces no flow rather than a burst pipe — although the liquid churning in the casing will heat up fast. A positive displacement pump in the same situation will keep building pressure. Protection philosophy differs ac

Reciprocating. A plunger or piston reciprocating in a cylinder, with suction and discharge valves in the head. Gland packing contains the pressurised fluid. Plungers are commonly driven in pairs or threes off a common crankshaft (duplex, triplex) to smooth the delivery. Diaphragm. Fundamentally a plunger pump in which the plunger pressurises hydraulic oil, and the oil flexes a diaphragm that does the actual pumping. The process liquid never touches the drive, which is why diaphragm pumps are the default for hazardous and toxic duties. Critical services use a double diaphragm with a thin water film between the two and a pressure sensor in that gap: normally the gap pressure is zero, and when either diaphragm ruptures the sensor immediately sees full process discharge pressure. The process liquid still has not reached atmosphere. Rotary. Gear (external and internal), lobe, vane, progressive cavity, peripheral and screw. Each traps liquid in a cavity formed between rotating elements and the casing and carries it from suction to discharge. Liquid is carried in the tooth pockets and expelled as the teeth re-mesh. High-pressure hydraulics. Support on both sides of each gear keeps noise low. Internal gear A gear-within

Centrifugal pumps are divided by the direction the liquid leaves the impeller, which in turn is set by specific speed : Radial flow — the plain centrifugal pump, usually with a volute casing. Liquid enters at the impeller eye and is thrown radially outward. Low flow, high head. Mixed flow — the discharge direction lies between radial and axial. Axial flow — the rotor is a propeller and flow runs parallel to the shaft. High flow, low head. Other kinetic machines exist — electromagnetic, jet, gas-lift and hydraulic ram pumps — but they are outside the scope of this reference.

In a typical petroleum plant, 80–90% of all installed pumps are centrifugal. The reasons are structural rather than historical: simple construction, good efficiency over a wide flow and head range, smooth flow, and straightforward operation and maintenance. The basic machine is a volute and an impeller on a shaft carried by bearings in a bearing housing, with a coupling at the free end and a seal where the shaft passes through the casing. The modern centrifugal impeller traces to Denis Papin in 1689, who understood that vanes inside a spiral casing could create a forced vortex, though his vanes were straight. Combs published on curved vanes in 1838; Andrews introduced a proper volute casing in 1839 and a fully shrouded impeller in 1846. John Appold's systematic experiments culminated in his 1851 curved-blade pump, which reached 68% efficiency — a threefold improvement that established blade curvature as the key variable. The centrifugal pump only displaced positive displacement machines broadly once electric motors, steam turbines and internal combustion engines gave it a suitable high-speed driver. Normal operating speeds are 1500/1800 rpm and 3000/3600 rpm, corresponding to four- and two-pole motors on 50 and 60 Hz supplies. Specialised high-speed designs run from 5000 up to 25 000 rpm.

Every seal is a potential leak path, which is unacceptable for some liquids at any leak rate. Sealless designs eliminate the dynamic seal entirely by containing the whole rotor inside a pressure boundary. Canned motor pumps put the impeller, shaft and motor rotor inside the pump casing and a containment shell. The stator sits outside the shell and its rotating flux passes through the shell to drive the rotor. The hazardous liquid is confined by the shell and casing and also serves as the rotor coolant and bearing lubricant. Magnetic drive pumps keep the impeller, shaft and a set of driven magnets inside the containment shell. Drive magnets on a separate shaft outside the shell, coupled to the prime mover, turn the driven set through the shell wall. Field consideration Both sealless types depend on the pumped liquid for internal cooling and lubrication. Dry running, or operation at very low flow where the internal circulation collapses, destroys them quickly. They also tolerate solids and entrained gas poorly. The containment shell is the last pressure boundary, so its integrity monitoring matters as much as a seal plan does on a conventional pump.

Beyond the construction axes, pumps are built differently for the service they will see. The common application families are petroleum and chemical process, electric and nuclear power, water and wastewater, cooling tower, pulp and paper, slurry, pipeline and water-flood (injection), and high-speed pumps. Each brings its own material selection, impeller type, seal plan and testing expectations — the detail of which runs through the rest of this knowledge base.

For context on how broad the field is: water supply, drainage, sewage, irrigation, chemical and petroleum processing, pharmaceutical and medical (including the artificial heart), steel mills, construction dewatering and bypass pumping, and mining — tailings, dust control, groundwater control and site dewatering. Pumps also move whole potatoes, peel hazelnuts in chocolate manufacture, and drive waterjet cutting where a flame torch would be unsafe.

The parts that decide how a pump performs and how long it lasts: impellers, casings and diffusers, wear rings, shafts and sleeves, packing, mechanical seals, bearing housings and couplings. The basic components of a centrifugal pump are the same in nearly every design. What changes — and what decides whether a machine is fit for its duty — is how each component is constructed. This chapter works outward from the impeller. Impellers The impeller converts shaft rotation into liquid velocity. Liquid enters the eye , is guided from inlet to outlet by vanes , and leaves at the periphery. The vanes are normally cast integrally with a back plate (the back shroud or back cover) and, in closed designs, a front plate. Impellers are almost always castings; fabricated and welded impellers are rare. The casting process is where impeller quality is won. Liquid-contact surfaces must be as smooth as possible, so the core sand mixture and the core finish matter directly — the relative smoothness of the liquid path is one of the largest determinants of pump efficiency. Disk friction losses scale with roughly the fifth power of diameter , so a large closed impeller with a rough surface is penalised severely. After casting and surface finishing, impellers are dynamically balanced. ISO 1940 specifies residual unbalance limits; API imposes stricter ones. Balancing the impeller alone is not sufficient — once the rotor components are ready they should be mounted assembly-wise on the balancing machine and balanced as an assembly.

Liquid leaves the impeller outlet at 30–40 m/s. It must reach the discharge pipe at 3–7 m/s. That velocity reduction — and the conversion of kinetic energy into pressure — happens in the casing, in a device generically called a recuperator . Doing it with minimal loss is the whole design problem. The recuperator options are: vaneless guide ring, concentric casing, volute casing, vaned diffuser ring, diagonal diffuser vanes and axial diffuser vanes.

Two smooth discs with constant spacing, or spacing increasing toward the outlet. Pressure recovery is proportional to the ratio of outlet to inlet diameter (D o /D i ); ring breadth plays little part in head generation, though constant-breadth rings prove more efficient than those widening at outlet. Because high head would demand an impractically large outlet diameter, vaneless guide rings are confined to low-head pumps — typically mixed-flow impellers at higher specific speed with a constant-section annular delivery passage, and occasionally low specific speed pumps handling solids.

Found in single-stage pumps and in the last stage of multistage pumps. Impeller diameter to casing diameter ratio is held between 1.15 and 1.2 . Volute width accommodates the maximum impeller width; capacity at best efficiency is controlled by the volute diameter. A cutwater tongue minimises recirculation in the volute and significantly reduces radial load on the shaft. Below N s 600 (US units) a concentric casing is more efficient than a conventional volute; above 600 its efficiency falls away progressively. Choose a concentric casing when: flow is low and head high, with N s in the 500–600 range; one casing must accommodate several impeller sizes; the casing is fabricated rather than cast; the volute passage must be machined from a casting; foundry limitations force a wider impeller. Counter-intuitive behaviour In a concentric casing, uniform velocity and pressure distribution occurs at zero flow , and uniformity is progressively lost as flow rises — so radial load at BEP is considerably higher than at no-flow. This is the exact opposite of a volute casing. See Chapter 04 .

The most common design. With smooth surfaces, hydraulic losses are negligible, and impeller vanes and shrouds can be trimmed with minimal efficiency penalty. Kinetic energy converts to pressure only in the diffusion chamber immediately past the volute throat, where the divergence angle is between 7° and 13° . Volute cross-sections are circular, trapezoidal (typical of single-stage pumps) or rectangular. Rectangular sections are used in small single-stage and in multistage pumps; they are economical because pattern cost and production time are low, and hydraulic losses are minimal below N s 1100. Single versus double volute A single volute designed on constant velocity is the most efficient of all casing types, easy to cast and least expensive. Its weakness is radial load: pressure distribution is balanced only at BEP. At low flow, impeller surfaces nearest the discharge see high pressure while those beyond the cutwater see comparatively low pressure. The resulting unbalanced force can be taken as acting at a point 240° from the cutwater , directed toward the impeller centre, and is maximum at shut-off and almost zero at BEP. A double volute is two single volutes in opposed arrangement, with total throat area equal to the comparable single volute. It limits radial force substantially. The volute is symmetrical about its centreline, but the two passages carrying liquid to the dis

A ring of symmetrically placed vanes around the impeller forming gradually widening passages; flow from the diffuser is collected in a volute or circular casing. The narrowest section of each passage is the throat . Design parallels the volute, except that a diffuser has many throats where a volute has one continuous expanding section. Past the throat the channel area increases progressively, giving a further slight pressure rise. A straight diffusing channel is marginally more efficient but produces a larger casing. Vane count convention: the number of diffuser vanes is usually one more than the number of impeller vanes. Diffuser vanes should not greatly outnumber impeller vanes, and the one-more rule ensures a single impeller passage does not span several diffuser passages. Velocity distribution around the impeller is more uniform than in a volute, so radial loads are much lower.

Diagonal diffuser vanes serve mixed-flow impellers. They turn the liquid leaving the impeller to run along the pump axis, and reduce velocity to recover pressure. Vanes are disposed axially with no sudden area changes, which allows one diffuser model to serve impellers of different diameters and breadths. As specific speed rises, impeller and diffuser profiles approach propeller-pump shapes. Axial diffuser vanes sit behind the impeller of an axial flow pump, serving the same two functions. They usually number 5–8, with the lower count on lower specific speed pumps. Efficiency is influenced by passage shape — vane count, axial length and the gap between impeller blades and diffuser vanes. Shorter vanes in greater number give better efficiency for the same duty. At high enough specific speed the vanes become superfluous and a simple conical diffuser replaces them.

The impeller rotates inside a stationary casing, so a running clearance is unavoidable — and because there is a pressure difference across it, pumped liquid recirculates through it. That leakage costs efficiency. Tightening the clearance improves efficiency, reduces erosion from suction recirculation, and improves rotor-dynamic stability (so the pump runs with lower vibration). But it increases the risk of impeller-to-casing contact, which can scrap two expensive parts. The answer is to fit sacrificial rings : an impeller wear ring on the impeller eye and a case wear ring in the casing. Wear is then confined to cheap, replaceable components. Rings at the impeller eye are front wear rings. Rings are also fitted at the back shroud, typically when the impeller carries balancing holes to reduce axial thrust — see Chapter 04 .

The governing requirement is resistance to seizure on contact . Materials with galling tendencies — SS 316 notably — are therefore not used here. Favoured materials include: Austenitic grey iron castings — ASTM A436 Type 1 Austenitic ductile iron castings — ASTM A439 Type D2 12% chrome steel — AISI 420 (hardenable) 18Cr–8Ni steel castings — AISI 304 Copper alloy sand castings (bronze) — ASTM B584 Alloy C90500 Aluminium bronze sand castings — ASTM B148 Alloy C95800 Monel K500, Nickel 200 Hardness is deliberately mismatched so wear concentrates on the stationary part: case ring at roughly 225–275 BHN , impeller ring 50–100 BHN harder , in the 325–375 BHN range. Thermoplastic composite rings Thermoplastic composites — often carbon-fibre reinforced — are increasingly used, either on the stationary part alone or with a steel mating component. They are non-galling, have a lower coefficient of friction, and show excellent wear resistance in clean liquids. The greater hardness differential lets the thermoplastic act as the sacrificial element, and the reduced galling tendency allows roughly half the clearance that metal rings require — a direct efficiency gain, particularly on low specific speed pumps. Their limitations: maximum life is obtained only in clean fluids, and chemical compatibility is narrower than metals.

The rotor assembly comprises shaft, impeller, sleeves, the rotating seal element, bearings or bearing surfaces, and coupling half. The shaft is its key element and is a genuinely stressed member: during operation it sees tension, compression, bending and torsion, all cyclic — so fatigue is the expected failure mode . Shaft design is based either on torsional shear stress at the smallest diameter or, properly, on a comprehensive fatigue evaluation combining the loads, cycle count and stress concentration factors — invariably by finite element analysis. Stress is not the only criterion; the design must also satisfy: shaft deflection (see Chapter 04 ); key stresses; mounted component fits; critical speeds — rotordynamics. Mechanical seals and gland packing in contact with the shaft cause wear by friction and fretting corrosion. A shaft sleeve is fitted as a sacrificial component so the seal or packing runs against the sleeve, not the shaft — it is far cheaper to replace a sleeve than a complete shaft. Sleeve material generally mirrors the shaft, though standardisation favours SS 316. The portion exposed to the secondary seal (an O-ring or PTFE wedge) is hard coated: plasma-sprayed chrome oxide, tungsten carbide or alumina, giving around 70–72 HRc , then ground to finish. This is the area most prone to fretting.

A stuffing box is the chamber sealing the shaft where it passes through the casing. It holds 4–6 packing rings and a gland (end plate) that squeezes them down onto the shaft. The narrow annulus between shaft and packing is a restrictive path: it produces the pressure drop that prevents leakage, and considerable friction that heats the shaft. Operating practice Tighten the gland just enough to allow a slight, deliberate leak . That leakage is the packing's lubricant and coolant. A dry-tightened gland runs hot and wears the shaft or sleeve rapidly. In a properly operating stuffing box, friction losses run about 1% of total pump power , independent of pump size and type. Obviously this cannot be allowed on hazardous or toxic liquids — which is precisely why gland packing is not used on those services.

Lantern ring — a ring drilled circumferentially that replaces one packing ring, positioned at the pump end or midway through the packing set. Used for dirty or high-pressure liquid, it admits clean sealing liquid into the packing set. Throat (restrictive) bush — fitted at the stuffing box throat where discharge pressure is high. Water jacket — integrally cast into the stuffing box for liquids above about 120 °C , allowing cooling water circulation to keep the packing temperature down. Repeller (auxiliary impeller) — radial blades on the back shroud of an auxiliary impeller that throw liquid outward and so reduce the pressure in front of the packing. Used for toxic or corrosive liquids where complete sealing is necessary. The pressure it generates depends on blade length and casing clearance. Back vanes — cast on the main impeller itself, serving the same pressure-relief function. Work done against packing friction is influenced by packing quality and type, gland length, shaft diameter, rotational speed, pressure acting on the gland, and the volume of liquid passing through the packing.

Present-day pump packing is predominantly PTFE (Teflon) / graphite filament , braided and formed into square section, chosen for heat dissipation and low friction. Additional materials are braided in to handle specific conditions — contaminants, acids, alkalis, temperature and speed. Aramid , for example, enhances mechanical properties, resisting packing extrusion and standing up to slurries and abrasives.

Gland packing has three persistent disadvantages: it leaks continuously and loses product if the shaft surface is not smooth; over-tightening heats the shaft or sleeve and wears it rapidly; and it needs constant supervision. As a result, packing is being phased out except on non-critical, low-power duties. Most applications use mechanical seals. A mechanical seal comprises two perfectly lapped mating faces , one stationary and one rotating. The crucial conceptual difference from packing: in packing the leakage resistance acts along the shaft axis; in a mechanical seal it acts orthogonal to it. Seal faces cannot run against each other dry — that causes early wear, and seal damage means leakage. Sealant fluid is injected into the seal housing at a specified pressure to lubricate and cool the faces. Fluid escaping between the faces to atmosphere is fugitive emission ; where that is unacceptable, multiple seal arrangements are used. Seals are precision devices and demand corresponding care during pump assembly.

Every mechanical seal installation has three: At the mating surfaces of the primary and mating rings — the primary sealing face . Between the rotating component and the shaft or sleeve — a secondary seal . Between the stationary component and the gland plate — a secondary seal. A seal mounted on a sleeve adds a fourth point between shaft and sleeve, and some mating ring designs add a seal between gland plate and stuffing box. Mating faces are normally dissimilar materials , held in contact by a spring whose preload keeps the primary and mating rings together during shutdown or whenever liquid pressure is absent.

t: Why the secondary seal must be dynamic
b: The secondary seal between shaft and sleeve must be partially dynamic . As the faces wear, the primary ring has to creep forward. Machine vibration, shaft runout and differential thermal expansion between shaft and casing all require the secondary seal to move along the shaft. That flexibility comes from the secondary seal form — O-ring, wedge, V-ring or bellows. Most designs fix the seal head to the sleeve or shaft and provide positive drive to the primary ring.

Single seal — internally or externally mounted. A single seal mounted inside the seal chamber represents at least 75% of all installations and is the most economical sealing system available. Dual seal — tandem seals, or double seals (externally or internally pressurised).

Seals are housed in seal housings the way packing is housed in stuffing boxes. Research shows an enlarged bore confers distinct advantages: fluid flow within the enlarged chamber increases, which aids removal of seal-generated heat. Properly selected enlarged chambers help deal with: gas in the seal housing under start/stop conditions; light hydrocarbons with low boiling points; liquids carrying solid particles.

These normally use anti-friction bearings only. The radial ball or cylindrical roller bearing sits inboard, adjacent to the impeller, arranged to take radial load only. The thrust bearing sits closest to the coupling — usually a duplex pair of angular contact bearings or a double-row angular contact bearing. Ball bearing inboard → outboard is a duplex angular contact pair face to face , or a double-row angular contact bearing. Cylindrical roller bearing inboard → outboard pair mounted back to back so axial thrust can be carried in either direction. This duplex pair takes both the unbalanced axial thrust and radial load.

Radial and thrust bearings have individual housings. The radial bearing is normally at the coupling end; the ball thrust bearing is at the outboard end. The thrust bearing must be secured axially on the shaft to transmit load through the bearing to the housing — usually located against a shaft shoulder and locked with a bearing nut. That makes the shaft diameter under the thrust bearing smaller than under the radial bearing. Mounting the radial bearing at the inboard (coupling) end therefore gives a larger shaft diameter where torque has to be transmitted from the coupling to the impeller — the shaft under the outboard thrust bearing can be relatively small because no torque passes through it. The thrust bearing is locked axially in its housing; the radial bearing is left axially loose in its housing to permit thermal growth. A popular arrangement for in-between-bearing double-suction pumps is journal radial bearings plus a ball thrust bearing . All radial load goes to the journal bearings. The ball thrust bearing is mounted so it carries axial load only, with the housing radially loose around it and a metallic strap on the outer rings locking into the housing to prevent outer-ring rotation. This suits higher horsepower and higher speed duty where ball radial bearings would be impractical on speed, load or lubrication limits.

In vertical pumps the thrust bearing carries the unbalanced axial hydraulic force plus the static weight of the rotating element. By design it may sit in the driver or, more usually, at the head end within the pump casing. Bearing types range from ordinary ball, angular contact and split inner race angular contact up to spherical roller thrust bearings on large machines such as vertical deep well pumps. These bearings are typically rated for at least three times the maximum calculated thrust load, because so many factors are uncertain: thrust calculation is not highly accurate; thrust increases as internal clearances increase; thrust varies with the vertical position of the impellers in the casings; thrust varies with flow, and may even reverse direction. The most severe thrust loads occur at shutdown and from impact loading caused by water hammer. A reasonable margin between the driver thrust bearing rating and the maximum calculated pump thrust is essential.

Seal life and bearing life are coupled. Liquid leaking from a mechanical seal can fail the bearings; a bearing in poor condition shortens seal life. The blunt reality: only about 10% of rolling element bearings achieve their 3–5 year design life. Rain, product leakage, debris and wash-down water entering the bearing housing contaminate the lubricant, and the effect is catastrophic: 0.002% water in oil −48 % bearing life 0.10% water in oil −90 % bearing life End seals protect the housing — but in almost every case the end seal's own life and quality is far below that of the bearings it protects. Improving the end seal directly extends bearing life. The quantitative core of pump engineering — head, flow and system resistance, efficiency and power, the characteristic curve and its corrections, specific speed, and the cavitation, recirculation and NPSH behaviour that destroys more impellers than anything else. A centrifugal pump energises a liquid and delivers whatever flow the system will accept at the head it can generate. Understanding that exchange means being fluent in a small set of liquid properties and pump parameters. This chapter covers them, then builds to the single most consequential topic in pump engineering: suction conditions. t: Flow and head: the two things that do not change with liquid
b: The single most useful idea in this chapter A centrifugal pump is a volumetric machine. At one point of operation it delivers the same volume flow rate and generates the same head in metres of liquid column for any liquid — hydrocarbon, water, anything. What changes with density is the mass flow , the pressure gauge reading and the power . A 20 m³/h pump moves 20 t/h of water, but only 16 t/h of a hydrocarbon at SG 0.8 — same volume, same metres of head, 80% of the mass and 80% of the power. Flow is measured in m³/h, l/s or gpm (US or Imperial). Head is expressed in metres (or feet) of liquid column, mlc. The difference between discharge head and suction head is the differential head — what the pump actually produces. Not all the kinetic energy becomes pressure. Pump efficiency accounts for three loss groups, and is the product of three efficiencies: Hydraulic efficiency — chiefly disk friction (liquid against the impeller shrouds), a function of speed and impeller geometry, plus shock losses from rapid direction changes through impeller and volute. Volumetric efficiency — recirculation losses at wear rings, interstage bushes and similar leakage paths. Mechanical efficiency — friction at the seal or gland packing and at the bearings. The product of the first two is sometimes called internal efficiency . Every pump is designed for one flow and one corresponding head; efficiency is maximum there and that point is the Best Efficiency Point (BEP) . Efficiency falls away at every other flow. Every manufacturer supplies a characteristic curve. It is four curves on one sheet, all plotted against capacity Q: Q vs H — capacity against differential head Q vs η — capacity against efficiency Q vs P — capacity against shaft power Q vs NPSH-r — capacity against required suction head

The Q–H curve droops continuously from shut-off (no flow) to BEP and beyond. API recommends the curve rise by at least 10% from BEP to shut-off for single-stage, single-pump operation. Any pump model can be assembled with trimmed impellers — usually not smaller than 20% below the maximum possible diameter. Trimmed-impeller Q–H curves run parallel to and below the maximum-diameter curve within the operating range. A curve sheet covering all available impeller diameters shows efficiency as iso-efficiency contours across the Q–H field. A small triangle on the curve marks the rated point — the flow and head the manufacturer guarantees. The rated flow is usually 5–10% above the normal operating point , which is the flow the process actually demands most of the time. Shut-off head is the head at zero flow, with the discharge valve closed and the liquid churning in the casing. Radial-impeller pumps are started this way, but run time in that condition must be minimised — see temperature rise .

Q vs η is an inverted U: zero at no flow, rising to a maximum at BEP, then dropping. Flows above and below BEP produce higher hydraulic losses and therefore lower efficiency. Q vs P is obtained by test on cold water. Because volume flow in m³/h, head in metres and efficiency are all independent of the liquid, the test result is valid for every service liquid — the power simply scales by specific gravity. Q vs NPSH-r is the measured suction head at which throttling the suction produces a 3% drop in differential head at that flow. NPSH-r depends on the service liquid, but cold water is the most damaging of the commonly pumped liquids, so NPSH-r measured on cold water can be safely applied to hydrocarbons and hot water.
Curves are generated on cold water at one speed and one impeller diameter. Real service changes at least one of those. Factors let you predict performance without retesting.

The Sabini and Fraser curves (1986 Pump Users Symposium) assumed: single-stage pumps only; finish and dimensional tolerance within ±1% for vanes and hydraulic passages; wetted surface finish of 2 × 10⁻⁶ per inch of impeller diameter or better; wear ring clearance of 0.0015 in per inch of ring diameter; suction specific speed not exceeding 8500 (US units); discharge recirculation within 80–90%; uniform velocity profile at impeller inlet; clean water at 150 °F or below; efficiency based on maximum impeller diameter; wet-pit efficiencies based on impellers without back rings or balancing holes. Lobanoff and Ross studied pumps of six stages or fewer at 3560 rpm and found efficiency rising very rapidly to N s ≈ 2000, holding roughly constant to about 3500, then tapering. The explanation is structural: hydraulic friction and shock losses are a greater share of total head in high-N s pumps, while mechanical losses barely change across the range and so dominate the power budget at low N s .

A related index used for very large pumps in hydroelectric work: two geometrically similar pumps working against the same head will have similar flow conditions — the same velocities at all sections — if they run at speeds inversely proportional to their size . Capacity then varies as the square of the size.

As liquid is drawn into the pump inlet, the pressure acting on it falls. When the reduced pressure approaches the liquid's vapour pressure at that temperature , the liquid vaporises. Those vapour bubbles travel into the impeller, where pressure rises again and they collapse — implode . That implosion is cavitation. Damage ranges from minor pitting to catastrophic failure, depending on fluid characteristics, energy level and duration. It occurs mostly within the impeller, specifically on the leading face of the non-pressure side of the vanes , where bubbles begin to collapse and release their energy. The signature is a pockmarked, rough surface and severe thinning of the vanes by metal erosion.

t: Recirculation — a different mechanism, often misdiagnosed
b: Recirculation is flow reversal at the inlet or outlet tips of the impeller vanes. Cavitation-type damage on the inlet vanes that is not associated with inadequate NPSH can be traced directly to operation in the suction recirculation zone; similar damage at the discharge vane tips to the discharge recirculation zone. The capacities at which suction and discharge recirculation begin are set by the impeller inlet and outlet design respectively. The casing influences the intensity of discharge recirculation but not its inception . Research shows that when the impeller inlet-to-outlet diameter ratio equals or exceeds 0.5, the suction recirculation capacity is effectively also the discharge recirculation capacity. How suction recirculation becomes cavitation Operating left of BEP, eddy currents form at the impeller eye. Flow rate through the pump has not dropped — but the eddies effectively reduce the flow channel area. Same flow through a smaller area means higher velocity; higher velocity means a larger friction pressure drop; and when that drop takes the local pressure below vapour pressure, the pump experiences classical cavitation initiated by recirculation . A second explanation: as fluid flows over a vane the near-surface pressure falls and flow tends to separate. Separation occurs once the incidence angle — the difference between flow angle and vane inlet angle — exceeds a cr

Two quantities, constantly confused: NPSH-r — Net Positive Suction Head required by the pump to prevent the inception of cavitation and give safe, reliable operation. A property of the pump. NPSH-a — Net Positive Suction Head available from the suction system. A property of the installation. This field is still, as the literature frankly admits, misunderstood, misapplied and misused — producing either costly over-design of new systems or unreliable operation of existing ones.

t: NPSH-r: what the number actually means
b: The Hydraulic Institute defines NPSH-r as the NPSH that causes total head (first-stage head on a multistage pump) to be reduced by 3% due to flow blockage from cavitation vapour in the impeller vanes. It is a practical, repeatable test definition. The most important caveat in pump engineering NPSH-r by the 3% definition is not the point at which cavitation starts. That level is incipient cavitation , and the NPSH at incipient cavitation can be 2 to 20 times the 3% NPSH-r value depending on pump design — the higher ratios on high-suction-energy pumps or pumps with large impeller inlet areas. If NPSH-a merely equals NPSH-r, the pump does not make rated head: it makes 3% less, and it is cavitating. Suction energy level rises with: casing suction nozzle size; pump speed; suction specific speed; specific gravity of the pumped liquid. Anything that increases velocity in the impeller eye, the pump's flow rate, or specific gravity increases suction energy. Most standard low -suction-energy pumps can operate with little or no margin above NPSH-r without seriously affecting service life. High-suction-energy pumps cannot. Theoretical, cavitation-free NPSH-r A theoretical NPSH-r that genuinely indicates cavitation inception is built from three loss groups: head loss due to friction, head drop due to fluid acceleration, and head loss due to improper fluid entry into the impeller blade. t: Why cold water is the worst case
b: Vapour formation during cavitation or recirculation is a thermal process and depends on liquid properties: pressure, temperature, specific heat and latent heat of vaporisation. For liquid to boil, the latent heat must come out of the liquid flow. The extent of cavitation depends on the proportion of vapour released, how fast it is liberated, and the vapour's specific volume. This is captured in a gas-to-liquid ratio factor C b (Vlaming, ASME 81-WA/FE-32). The conclusion: cold water has the greatest potential to cause cavitation damage of the commonly pumped liquids , and cold water is worse than hot water — the specific volume of vapour falls rapidly as pressure and temperature rise. Field experience agrees: pumps on hydrocarbons or hot water operate satisfactorily at lower NPSH-a than cold water demands. Which is convenient, because it means pumps tested on cold water are good enough for those services.

t: What the research actually says about NPSH
b: Terry Henshaw compiled the findings of many investigators in Predicting NPSH for Centrifugal Pumps . The practical conclusions: The industry standard defines NPSH-r as NPSH-a with cool water that creates enough cavitation in the impeller eye to drop one-stage head by 3%. Because of the 3% definition, a pump with a larger diameter impeller requires less NPSH than the same pump with a smaller one. NPSH required to achieve 100% head is typically 1.05–2.5× the 3% NPSH-r. NPSH required to suppress all cavitation is typically 4–5× the 3% NPSH-r, though the ratio can range from 2 to 20. "Incipient" cavitation causes minimal impeller damage. The peak erosion rate occurs between the 3% NPSH-r value and the incipient-cavitation value — not at either end. For cool-water service, the 3% head-drop NPSH is not sufficient to prevent cavitation erosion of the impeller. At BEP, NPSH-r does not vary with speed to the exponent 2 — the exponent is more typically 1.5 . Consequently N ss at BEP increases as speed increases. NPSH-r curve shape varies with the percentage head drop used. The 3% curve decreases as flow decreases, reaching a minimum at or below 40% of BEP; the 1% and 0% curves increase as flow falls below BEP. Axial thrust and radial load — where they come from, how each impeller and casing arrangement manages them, and how shaft deflection translates them into seal and bearing failures. A centrifugal pump delivers a wide range of flows and heads. The operating point on the curve, and the internal pressures that result, produce axial and radial forces on the rotor. Those forces select the bearings, size the shaft, and — through shaft deflection — determine how long the seals last. This chapter covers where they come from and how each construction manages them. Axial thrust Axial thrust arises from internal pressures acting on the exposed areas of the rotating element. It looks like it should be simply the net of discharge and suction pressure times the exposed impeller area — and that is indeed the basis — but several variables are not captured by that approach: location of the impeller relative to the casing wall; impeller shroud symmetry; surface roughness of the walls; wear ring clearance; geometry of the balancing holes. Axial thrust arises from internal pressures acting on the exposed areas of the rotating element. It looks like it should be simply the net of discharge and suction pressure times the exposed impeller area — and that is indeed the basis — but several variables are not captured by that approach: location of the impeller relative to the casing wall; impeller shroud symmetry; surface roughness of the walls; wear ring clearance; geometry of the balancing holes. Calculated thrust is approximate Many of these variables are indeterminate, so calculated axial forces are at best approximate. In critical applications, during prototype testing, or when troubleshooting repeated thrust bearing failures, install thrust-measuring devices and record internal pressures directly. If the measured results are unacceptable, the design needs modification — not a bigger bearing.

The impeller profile is symmetrical. The impeller centreline coincides reasonably with the volute centreline — within 0.8 mm . Pressure on the front cover and back shroud is equal and constant from the impeller OD down to the wear ring diameter. The parabolic pressure reduction across the shrouds is ignored; the average pressure acting on the shrouds is taken as ¾ of discharge pressure .

Theoretically a double-suction impeller develops almost no axial thrust, by symmetry. In practice construction is never perfectly symmetrical, so some thrust always exists and a simple thrust bearing absorbs it. Alignment is not optional here The symmetry that gives the double-suction impeller its balance requires the impeller outlet to stay aligned with the volute centre . Violate that and substantial thrust is generated — proportional to the axial displacement . This is a direct assembly and overhaul check item.

With all impellers stacked facing the same direction, the axial thrust pushing the rotor toward the suction can be very high. Such designs carry a balancing drum or piston : a rotating disk running against a stationary disk or ring at close clearance. The liquid pressure drops across that labyrinth passage, and the leakage is piped back to the pump suction. Pressure difference across the drum equals the net of discharge and suction pressure, and the resulting force opposes the thrust on the rotor. The arrangement also reduces the pressure acting on the stuffing box. The cost is efficiency: liquid recirculating through the balance line is lost work.

Arranging impellers back to back simplifies axial balance for odd or even stage counts. Two locations on the rotor each break down half the total pump head: the centre bushing between the back-to-back impellers, and the throat bush in the high-pressure stuffing box. Sleeve diameters at those two locations can be sized to balance any number of stages. Practical rules for this arrangement: It is preferable to leave some residual axial thrust so the bearing stays lightly loaded and the rotor is held in one place rather than allowed to float. An increase in wear ring or bush clearance does not affect axial thrust in this design — a genuine reliability advantage over the stacked arrangement. All impeller rings should be the same diameter . On even-stage pumps, the centre sleeve diameter should equal the sleeve diameters in each stuffing box. To balance an odd number of stages, the simplest solution is to change only the centre sleeve diameter.

In an end-suction pump with an overhung impeller, hydraulic radial load comes from non-uniform liquid velocity within the casing , which produces a non-uniform pressure distribution around the impeller circumference. The volute design is the dominant influence. The volute is sized for flow at BEP, and at that flow velocity and pressure distribution in the casing are uniform, so radial thrust is negligible. The small residual load at BEP comes from the cutwater , which necessarily disturbs the pressure distribution; that force is directed toward the cutwater. At flows above or below BEP the magnitude of the radial force increases — and its direction also changes . Vane pass excitation. A fluctuating radial load arises when the clearance between impeller vane tips and the volute cutwater is too small. The resulting vibration occurs at the vane pass frequency = number of impeller vanes × pump running speed. This is a diagnostic signature, and the cure is a correct Gap-B . Mechanical imbalance of the rotor generates a radial force at running speed. Uneven flow through the impeller can itself cause impeller imbalance. Cavitation , and misaligned belts or couplings , also contribute radial load to the shaft.

A radial load — hydraulic or from mechanical imbalance — bends the shaft downward in one position. Rotate the shaft 180° and it still bends downward in the same way. That bending under a constant unidirectional load is deflection : the deflected shaft rotates about its own centreline even though that centreline is not straight. The consequence is a reversal of stress in the shaft on every revolution , which leads to fatigue cracking and eventual shaft breakage. Deflection versus whip Shaft whip is a different motion: the shaft end orbits, generating a cone, and the shaft centreline itself shifts 180° for every 180° of shaft rotation. Whip comes from rotordynamic problems; radial load contributes little to it. The two are regularly confused, and they have different cures.

Rubbing contact. Rotating parts may touch stationary parts. Stainless steel parts gall as soon as rubbing contact is made, which shows up as motor overload. Galling tends to get progressively worse and can end in complete seizure of the rotating element. The first surfaces to touch are the wear rings — whose clearance is deliberately minimised to maximise the pressure drop across them — or, on pumps without wear rings, the shaft against the stuffing box throat bush. Packing leakage. Conventional packing adjusted for the deflection at one operating condition will not readjust when the deflection changes. Set the packing at the high-capacity end of the curve, then throttle the discharge: the shaft moves from one extreme position to the other, leaving a gap between packing and shaft. That gap plus the elevated stuffing box pressure near shut-off produces excessive leakage. Seal face misalignment. On a mechanically sealed pump, deflection causes facial misalignment of the seal faces. The faces either open up or mate unevenly, producing uneven and early wear and then leakage. Reading and using the four characteristic curves: curve stability and steepness, why the H–Q and P–Q curves take the shape they do, parallel and series operation, speed–torque at start-up, flow regulation, and the limits of the allowable operating region. A centrifugal pump's most attractive feature is its ability to perform across a wide range of operating conditions — flow rate, suction and discharge head, speed, and liquid type and properties. But it is designed for one discrete combination of flow, head and speed: the Best Efficiency Point. In practice a pump is rarely operated at the parameters it was designed for, so what matters is knowing how it responds when conditions move. Consider a pump discharging into the bottom of an elevated vessel. As the vessel fills, the differential head the pump must generate rises, and as H rises, Q falls. If power demand rises with it, the load on the motor may pull the driver speed down. Process and utility duties that span a wide flow and head range may demand several pumps running together in one system — where each pump's performance is affected by the others. t: How specific speed shapes the curves
b: Specific speed has a strong influence on the character of all four curves. The shapes look different between a low-N s radial pump and a high-N s propeller pump, but the trends are consistent and worth committing to memory. For a radial impeller pump the P–Q curve rises with flow, so minimum power is at zero flow — start with the discharge valve closed. For a propeller (axial flow) pump the power curve falls with flow, so minimum power is at full flow — start with the discharge valve fully open. There is a second reason for axial pumps: the hydraulics become unstable at 70–75% of BEP , and on a closed valve the torque reaches normal value before full speed is obtained. Axial and mixed-flow pump flow is therefore rarely throttled at all.
H–Q curves come in two kinds, and the distinction decides whether the pump can be used in parallel.
Differential head falls progressively as flow increases. The shut-off head H SO is the maximum head the pump will ever develop. One system head corresponds to exactly one flow.

Head rises from H SO to a maximum at some intermediate flow, then falls. The consequence is that for one system head requirement H₁ there are two possible flow rates , Q₁ and Q₂. What an unstable curve does in service With a head requirement above H SO , pump flow oscillates between Q₁ and Q₂ , giving a modulating flow rate and pipeline vibration. This is not a theoretical concern; it is a recognisable field symptom. Stability in a single-stage pump can be obtained by: reducing the number of vanes; modifying the vane geometry; reducing the vane outlet angle; on multistage pumps, modifying the diffuser shape and return vanes. API 610 requirement API 610 requires that all pumps have stable H–Q curves — head at rated capacity must rise continuously until it reaches shut-off head. For parallel operation of single- or double-stage pumps the head rise from rated capacity to shut-off must be 10–20% . For three or more stages a lower percentage is permitted, because the same percentage would produce excessively high shut-off heads.

Steepness is associated with a stable curve and is defined as the percentage rise in head from BEP to shut-off: Steepness % = (H SO − H BEP ) ⁄ H BEP × 100 Alternatively expressed as the ratio ΔH/ΔQ. Small ΔH/ΔQ is a flat characteristic; large ΔH/ΔQ is a steep one. Steepness is set by the number of vanes and the blade outlet angle . Practical industry combinations run roughly from 3 vanes at 17° through 8 vanes at 28°, with the higher vane counts and angles showing droop. The application decides which is wanted. One or many hydrants may open at once, so the required flow can increase sharply and without warning. As flow rises the pressure from the pump must not drop substantially , because a drop in delivered head directly reduces the height to which water can be thrown. Hence the flat characteristic requirement.

Comparing the triangles directly: Flow reduced → C u2 increases , C m2 decreases → head rises. Flow increased → C u2 decreases → head falls. The self-regulating property This is why the H–Q curve droops — and it gives centrifugal pumps their most valuable operational characteristic. If total head rises during operation, the pump automatically reduces its discharge so the impeller can overcome the increased resistance. Conversely, a reduction in delivery-pipe resistance stimulates the pump to increase discharge. No control system is involved; it is inherent in the velocity triangles.

t: The inlet velocity triangle and off-BEP losses
b: At the inlet, U₁ = π·N·d₁/60 is constant, C m1 = Q/area, and W₁ is the relative velocity. When flow changes, the angle of entry β 1-en changes relative to the fixed blade inlet angle β₁: Q < Q BEP → β 1-en < β₁ → flow separation, eddies on the inner surface of the vane; Q = Q BEP → β 1-en = β₁ → clean, shockless entry; Q > Q BEP → β 1-en > β₁ → eddies on the outer surface of the vane. In practice a certain pre-whirl exists, which reduces the mismatch between β 1-en and β₁ at off-BEP flows, so real losses are less than a straight-entry assumption predicts. These off-BEP flows also cause disturbance and hydraulic loss in the diffuser ring and volute casing. Conflicting loss exponents in the literature Sources describe off-BEP hydraulic losses as proportional to the square of flow in one place and the cube of flow in another. The qualitative point is what matters and is not in dispute: losses grow rapidly and non-linearly as the duty moves away from BEP in either direction. Do not rely on a specific exponent for a calculation.

t: The cause of the efficiency curve
b: Hydraulic losses occur at every flow other than BEP and grow as the duty moves away in either direction. The other two loss groups — recirculation losses and mechanical losses — are not greatly affected by flow. So there is one flow at which the sum of losses is minimum, and efficiency is maximum there. That produces the inverted-U efficiency curve.

Given the variety of pump types, sizes, flows, heads, powers and efficiencies, direct comparison between machines is difficult. Non-dimensional characteristics solve it, and they are necessary for transferring a known characteristic from one geometrically similar pump to another.

Take the normal operating point — the point the pump is supposed to operate at most of the time — and call its values Q n , H n , P n , η n . Treat each as 100% and express all deviations as percentages of normal. Once the normal values are known for a desired characteristic, the rest of the curve follows. The P–Q comparison across specific speeds earlier in this chapter is exactly this technique.

Everything above assumed constant speed. With a variable speed drive, the inlet and outlet velocity triangles remain similar and all velocities vary in proportion to speed. Hence the affinity laws : Q₁ ⁄ Q₂ = N₁ ⁄ N₂ · H₁ ⁄ H₂ = (N₁ ⁄ N₂)² · P₁ ⁄ P₂ = (N₁ ⁄ N₂)³ Head goes with u₂², hence with N². Power goes with Q×H, hence with N³. Valid only at constant efficiency ; divergence from practice becomes significant beyond ±25% speed change.

Take a point P on the Q–H curve at normal speed N, and its homologous points P₁ and P₂ at speeds N₁ and N₂. Resolving the affinity relations gives: H x = H × (Q x ⁄ Q)² A parabola through the origin . Every point on it has the same specific speed — substitute the proportional speeds into the N s equation and the result is a constant. These are constant specific speed curves . Because efficiency is a direct function of specific speed, every homologous point on one of these parabolas has the same specific speed and the same efficiency . That is the geometric reason iso-efficiency contours on a performance map are parabolic through the origin — and it is the basis for the impeller trim construction later in this chapter.

Two configurations: several pumps discharging into a common delivery pipe ( parallel — flows add at a common pressure), or pumps sharing the total head requirement ( series — heads add at a common flow). Addition is never as simple as it looks Total flow or total head is not a simple addition of individual values — especially where the pumps have dissimilar curves. The actual operating point is always set by where the combined pump curve intersects the system resistance curve .

Construct the combined curve by adding the abscissae (flows) at each head — for two identical pumps, double the flow at each head while holding head constant. It is tempting to assume that combined curve point is where the pair will operate. It is not. The operating point depends on system resistance. A single pump intersecting the resistance curve delivers Q c1 . Start the second pump and the resistance curve — which goes with Q² — turns upward steeply, intersecting the combined curve at Q c2 . The parallel pumping disappointment Q c1 is nowhere near half of Q c2 . Because system resistance rises with the square of flow, adding a second identical pump typically yields far less than double the flow. One documented example: two identical pumps that would each deliver 15.75 l/s produced only 18.5 l/s together instead of the naive 31.5 l/s, because the system pipework resistance dominated. The remedy is on the system side: size the pipework correctly to keep flow resistance low . If the resistance curve is steep, parallel pumping cannot help much however many pumps you add. Where the flow must be regulated, it is more efficient to throttle only one pump . With two dissimilar curves the combined characteristic has a kink. Until the operating point reaches the shut-off head of the higher -head pump, that pump delivers no flow at all — it sees shut-off conditions for itself. Only beyond that point does it begin contributing. Starting order matters With dissimilar curves in parallel, start the pump with the lower shut-off head first , then the higher one. Start them in the wrong order and one pump runs at shut-off, churning and heating, delivering nothing. The same trap appears when curves are very flat and one pump's shut-off head is only slightly lower than the other's.

t: Parallel operation, flat versus steep curves
b: Three combinations exist: both flat, both steep, one of each. Comparing the first two at the same differential head, the flow gain from starting the second pump (Q c − Q a ) is greater for flat curves than for steep ones. Pumps in parallel are therefore used wherever a flat characteristic (small dH/dQ) is wanted.

Construct the combined curve by doubling the head ordinate at each flow, holding flow constant. For dissimilar pumps the method is the same. At any instant the flow through both pumps must be the same . The total heads of the two pumps are equal only if their individual head–discharge characteristics are identical. Series operation of single-stage pumps is seldom encountered in practice — multistage centrifugal pumps are used instead.
As covered under viscosity corrections , higher viscosity reduces head, capacity and efficiency while increasing power. Use the Hydraulic Institute coefficients to derate the clean-liquid curve.

Suspended solids increase hydraulic resistance in proportion to their concentration in the liquid. The consequences: flow rate and head developed are both lower ; power required is higher ; efficiency is consequently lower . Where the particles are fine they form a broadly homogeneous mixture and the characteristic begins to resemble that of a higher-viscosity liquid — so viscosity correction thinking transfers across. Slurry curves must be measured Q–H curves for mixtures of water and solids — sand, slag, sugar beet, potatoes, fish — can only be determined by experiment . The practical approach is to compare measured curves at various solids percentages against clear water and build a nomogram, which can then predict performance for a particular mixture. There is no general correction chart.

Normal operation means rotation in the direction matching the impeller's backward-curved vanes, and flow from suction (lower head) to discharge (higher head). But four quadrants exist, and all four are encountered during start, stop or multi-pump operation. Together they form the complete characteristic of the pump. If head continues to rise — possible in parallel operation — liquid flows backward through the running pump. Reverse flow increases as discharge head rises above shut-off. −N, +Q Reverse rotation, normal flow Common when induction motor phase terminals are swapped. The pump still delivers from suction to discharge, but head and flow are substantially lower because efficiency in reverse rotation is poor. A classic commissioning fault. −N, −Q Reverse rotation, reverse flow The machine is acting as a hydraulic turbine — the head drop across the impeller converts to mechanical work. Seen when a system has no non-return valve, or a passing one, and the motor trips: liquid flows backward and the impeller spins in reverse. Pumps are driven machines, coupled to electric motors, IC engines, or steam or gas turbines. The prime mover must be rated and matched to the pump to ensure proper start-up — and that means knowing the pump's speed–torque (N–T) or mechanical characteristic. The N–T characteristic is plotted with torque as a percentage of nominal torque on the ordinate and speed as a percentage of nominal speed on the abscissa. Theoretically it is a parabola from the origin, proportional to speed squared: T = k·N² In practice a certain torque is required at zero speed to overcome mechanical losses in bearings, seals and packing and to accelerate the rotor inertia — so the actual curve starts above the origin. Curve shape depends on pump type and on whether the discharge valve is open or closed at start. Started with the discharge valve closed, a centrifugal pump demands 30–50% of nominal torque after reaching full speed — the exact value a function of specific speed and rotating mass. Mixed-flow pumps have more steeply falling N–Q characteristics than lower specific speed pumps.

The driver must deliver more torque than the pump demands at every speed from zero to full load. That excess is what accelerates the shaft to rated speed. Because a pump has a slow-rising N–T characteristic, most prime movers meet this requirement comfortably. A pump has to adapt to temporary and permanent changes in process demand. That variation is regulation , achieved either at constant speed or by varying speed. At constant speed: throttling the discharge valve, bypassing flow, changing impeller diameter, adjustable guide vanes, or modifying the impeller. Where several pumps run in one system, regulation may instead be achieved by stopping some of them — common for boiler feed water, cooling tower and similar utility duties.

The commonest method, manual or by control valve, and the simplest. But it is confined mostly to radial impeller, low specific speed pumps — as specific speed rises the P–Q curve flattens or droops, and throttling then saves no energy at all. Throttling is inefficient for four distinct reasons: the increased pressure drop across the closing valve is wasted energy ; introducing even a fully open control valve adds a dynamic head loss — typically taken as 10% of the other losses ; throttling shifts the system curve and moves the operating point along the Q–H curve away from BEP in either direction, reducing pump efficiency; control valve installations require bypass piping and isolation valves for valve repair. Use throttling where regulation is temporary or continuously changing . Where permanent regulation is wanted, modify the impeller instead.

Divert part of the discharge back to the pump suction or to another system — in effect splitting the pump flow between two systems of different resistance. Normally used on high specific speed pumps and on boiler feed water pumps with large demand variation.

Trimming the impeller brings a permanent change in flow and head. When outside diameter d₂ is reduced to d₂′, the outlet velocity triangle changes: peripheral velocity U₂ reduces and the outlet angle β₂ increases . Impeller width b₂, vane length and vane overlap all change too. Some pumps have inlet guide vanes, much like a centrifugal fan. Adjusting them induces pre-whirl in the liquid entering the impeller, which changes flow and head. Positive pre-whirl (liquid rotating with the impeller) is suitable for regulation: increasing pre-whirl reduces flow and discharge head. Negative pre-whirl is unsuitable — it reduces pump efficiency. Effectiveness depends strongly on specific speed: pre-whirl regulation is not very effective in low specific speed pumps and improves as specific speed rises. Outlet guide vane designs also exist.

In propeller pumps, variable-pitch blades change flow and head by altering the blade inclination angle (β + α) without changing diameter. Reducing the angle reduces discharge without an appreciable drop in efficiency , and the change in head is also not substantial.

The most economical method: no throttling losses, and minimal deviation from rated efficiency. The key distinction from throttling is which curve moves — throttling shifts the system resistance curve ; speed variation moves the pump Q–H curve along the system resistance curve. Energy supplied to the pump reduces with speed, whereas throttling and bypass supply full energy even at a reduced operating point. The drawbacks: effectiveness depends heavily on the shape of the pump curve; not all pump designs can be effectively speed-controlled — particularly those requiring recycle control; there is still some loss of pump efficiency, though far less than with throttling. The problems to the right of BEP are different. For low specific speed pumps the overloading power characteristic means power demand keeps rising, which ultimately trips the motor. The second problem is breakaway NPSH-r . At higher flow, internal fluid velocities are higher, and by Bernoulli the static head component falls — approaching vapour pressure. The static pressure must therefore be supplied externally, meaning a higher NPSH-r is required at higher flows. The margin closes from both ends Even where a pump has adequate NPSH margin at rated flow, at higher flows that margin can be consumed very rapidly — NPSH-a falls with rising friction loss while NPSH-r climbs. Beyond the breakaway point the margin can go negative , and the pump cavitates. This is the mechanism behind the otherwise baffling symptom of a pump that cavitates when NPSH-a is increased . Flow at 120% of BEP is sometimes called the end of the curve . Motor selection and sizing for low specific speed pumps is often done treating that as the last operating point on the curve — which is the correct conservative practice, since it is the maximum power the motor can be asked to deliver.

System analysis through to award: establishing boundary conditions and flow requirements, specifying the fluid and the criticality, writing the data sheet, issuing the bid request and scoring the bids. For some duties it is enough to buy a pump off the shelf on the horsepower rating of its motor or its overall dimensions. The fit to the application will not be ideal, but the penalty for a mismatch is small. In process industries that calculus reverses. Pumps perform vital functions continuously, in difficult environments, and the penalties attached to downtime and maintenance are significant. It becomes necessary to specify the process and its requirements properly, so that the selected pump is designed and manufactured to operate under the specified conditions reliably, efficiently and cost-effectively. Why the specification is the highest-leverage document A good pump specification is the foundation of pump reliability across its entire service life. It is the first document a user prepares for a pump, and it is often the most important. Failure to define or specify the pump complete
The first step. It comprises four evaluations: pump boundary conditions, flow requirements, fluid specification, and criticality of service.

The first boundary condition concerns the suction. From Chapter 03 , NPSH-a depends on: vapour pressure of the liquid; pipe losses; pressure in the suction vessel; gradient height; absolute (atmospheric) pressure. Location matters more than people expect Absolute pressure is constant for a location — which means you must know where the pump will be installed . This is a live issue when process and pump specifications are prepared for plants erected elsewhere in the world. Elevation above mean sea level determines the absolute pressure available; ambient temperature range and annual rainfall also determine some pump features. Suction line heat gain On pumps with a long suction pipe, heat added by heat-tracing lines and by ambient conditions raises the pumping temperature — and with it the vapour pressure of the liquid. Higher vapour pressure reduces NPSH-a . It may therefore be prudent to specify insulation on the suction piping , which is a specification decision, not a construction one. Fouling Long suction pipelines bring pipe losses, which are easy to compute. But some applications must also anticipate fouling of pipes, fittings and strainers. The extent of fouling before a cleanout must be estimated and accounted for — it both raises system resistance and drops NPSH-a . Fouling and Q max Fouling in the suction header steepens the droop in the NPSH-a curve, which reduces Q m

Where only minimal NPSH-a is available, note it clearly so that vendors offer pumps with low NPSH-r. But when they do, evaluate the suction specific speed of what is offered. A vendor can always buy you NPSH-r by enlarging the impeller inlet — and sell you a pump that cannot be turned down. As covered in Chapter 03 , N ss above 11 000 brings hydraulic and mechanical problems, especially at flows away from BEP. The basis is a statistical study of 480 refinery pumps over five years, presented by Jerry L. Hallam in 1982. The honest state of the N ss debate At the 13th International Pump Users Symposium (Texas A&M, 1996), Bernd Stoffel and Ralf Jaeger presented Experimental Investigations in Respect to the Relevance of Suction Specific Speed for the Performance and Reliability of Centrifugal Pumps . Three standard pumps of different specific speeds and sizes, from three German manufacturers, were each fitted alternately with a high-N ss impeller and one below the 11 000 limit. The measured quantities serving as indicators for dynamic loading of bearings and seals did not show trends or cause effects in the high-N ss pumps that would indicate higher failure probability. So a genuine debate exists over rejecting pumps above 11 000. NPSH-a evaluation more or less settles the suction side. The discharge side must be worked out the same way, considering: static head at the discharge — downstream pressure in the discharge vessel; the height that must be overcome to reach the discharge vessel; the rate of increase of system resistance with flow. That third item is easy to overlook and consequential. A quickly rising system resistance curve may preclude a maximum flow rate that is required occasionally — particularly where the maximum flow is far above the normal flow. Control valve sizing interacts with the pump Control valve sizing is based on the rate of rise of the system resistance curve as well as the pump size. The valve must provide the artificial head loss at the rated and minimum flow rates, and the minimum loss at the maximum flow rate . One way to flatten the system resistance curve is simply to install a larger pipe size — a decision that has to be made at specification stage, because nobody re-pipes a system to recover pump margin later. Evaluating suction and discharge resistance together gives the differential head required from the pump .

Flow is determined by process demand. A specification normally states two flow rates: Normal versus rated flow Definition Typical relationship Normal flow rate The flow at which the pump will usually operate. Baseline Rated flow rate The flow guaranteed by the vendor for the specified operating conditions. 10% above normal for low to medium flows; 5% above normal for higher flows Rated flow should reflect the maximum the system can envisage under current consideration, and should account for any anticipated future increase in process throughput. The minimum flow requirement may conflict with the rated flow. Where it does, make provision for recycle of the process liquid. Where possible, state the periods for which the pump will operate at minimum, maximum and rated flows — a long period at low flow implies higher radial loads, which greatly affects bearing life. Beyond minimum and maximum, the pump may be physically or hydraulically shut off at the discharge under certain operating conditions. Where that is the case, consider the minimum flow provisions from Chapter 05. Parallel operation deserves special care If the pump is required to operate in parallel with another, take great care to ensure minimum stable flows — especially where the Q–H curves are dissimilar . Criticality determines both the governing standard and the maintenance philosophy later. A pump is critical where any of the following apply: failure can affect plant safety and there is no standby ; the pump is vital for plant operation and its shutdown will curtail the process; it is part of a large horsepower train, where better operation can save energy or improve yields; capital cost is high, and it is very expensive to repair or has a long repair lead time; it is a perennial "bad actor" — a machine that wrecks on the slightest provocation of an off-duty operation. In most such cases a standby pump is specified, for a critical process on continuous operation. A specification trick worth knowing Sometimes the pump and its standby are specified with different types of driver — one on a steam turbine, the other on an electric motor. Process steam can then be utilised and power conserved, and the scheme ensures continued operation even on loss of power supply. Two benefits from one decision.

The bid request sends the data sheet to vendors for a quote. Guidelines: Send to three to five qualified vendors . Where the pump falls within standard offerings, three bids are sufficient. For specialised pumps, three to six. Enclose a covering form listing the mandatory and optional documents and their order . This acts as a checklist for the vendor and directly assists the bid evaluation that follows. Consider the user's existing inventory of pump spares when selecting vendors — similar pumps may be quoted that demand no additional spares. Conversely, a vendor may be excluded purely on poor follow-up and spares delivery . That is a legitimate commercial criterion. Professional courtesy that is also self-interest Preparing a bid consumes time, effort and money for the vendor, and reviewing it costs the user. Forward the bid request only to vendors whose bids will be seriously considered if their pumps meet the requirements. Padding the bid list to look diligent wastes everyone's budget and degrades the quality of the responses you get.

A clear, comprehensive specification is what lets a purchaser compare bids on an equal basis. Exceptions taken by vendors must be weighed and factored against the desired features and the prices offered. An analytical approach demands a tabulation of bids.

Bid analysis almost never produces a clear winner. Some pumps have an advantage in certain features and a disadvantage in others. The approach is to give weightage to all the factors and arrive at the pump scoring the most marks. Factorial weighting itself depends on many things — and a correct system analysis provides the sound basis for the weighting factors . A clear understanding of the pump's operating and system requirements leads to selection of a pump that will be efficient and reliable. Material specifications for pump components are usually based on API 610. In the 8th Edition, Table H-1 tabulates the material class for various pump components and Table H-2 provides the ASTM specifications. (Table designations change between editions — confirm against the edition in force.) The purchaser may alternatively specify materials from the liquid properties and reference the applicable ASTM, ANSI, AISI, BS, DIN or equivalent standard. Those standards provide the chemical composition limits and desired physical properties of the grade; ASTM, for example, specifies the tests to be run on the heat from which the material is supplied. Such tests are specifically recommended where: pump components are exposed to traces of hydrogen sulphide — in which case the materials of specific components must conform to NACE standard MR-01-75 (now MR0175/ISO 15156 — confirm the current designation); pumps are in highly corrosive or hazardous service; pumps are in low temperature applications — below −50 °C, though some specifications take −29 °C as the limit.

Special attention goes to the pressure-containing parts — pump casing and seal housings. These are usually castings, so special requirements apply to ensure component integrity. It is mandatory that castings are free from porosity, cracks, blowholes, shrink holes, scales and any other serious defect. Where a major defect is found in a casting for cryogenic service or in any special material, carry out the inspection in this order: check the mill test reports for chemical composition and physical properties; check any post-repair heat treatment charts ; check or witness the non-destructive examination as required and specified; check and review the welding procedures . Depending on size, rating and test specification, either the vendor's motor or the motor procured for the pump is used; it is aligned to the pump and electrically connected, and the suction and discharge piping is connected. Instrumentation is connected and activated. The pump is started and allowed to stabilise, and readings are taken once pump and motor temperatures flatten out. Data recorded at each point Shop test data set Hydraulic Flow rate · discharge pressure · suction pressure · elevation corrections · test fluid temperature · test fluid specific gravity Electrical Power reading · voltage at driver · current to driver · power factor · supply frequency Mechanical Vibration levels · bearing temperatures · noise levels · speed Usually five to seven test points are recorded, from near shut-off to 120% of rated flow . The points must include the normal and the rated flow rates . This is achieved by starting the pump with the discharge valve closed — the shut-off condition — then opening the valve in five to seven steps.

When collection is complete the data is tabulated. Corrections are computed for speed, density, viscosity and elevation. Corrected flow rates and differential head in metres of liquid column are entered, and power and efficiency are calculated for each point. The computation procedure is in Chapter 03 . Deviations are then checked against the acceptance criteria tolerances, and the tested performance curve is plotted from the collected data.
