When a running test fails the acceptance criteria, corrective action and possibly a retest follow. The common causes divide usefully into real pump problems and measurement problems — and it is worth establishing which before dismantling anything: Common causes of pump test failure Real pump problems Measurement and interpretation problems incorrect impeller diameter impeller with high residual imbalance unexpected seal failure rubbing at wear rings poor impeller surface quality uncalibrated instruments incorrect data collection and computational errors misinterpretation of test results and acceptance criteria

NPSH-r testing is done by one of two methods: Throttling the suction valve to reduce suction pressure; Pulling a vacuum in the suction vessel. The pump runs at constant flow rate and constant speed while suction pressure is reduced by either method. The reduction in suction head leads to a reduction in discharge head. For one flow rate, 5 to 12 readings may be taken and plotted; the set is then repeated for 1 to 4 flow rates. NPSH-r is read off as the suction head at which discharge head drops 3% from the rated head at that flow. Multistage pumps For a multistage pump the 3% drop is not taken on total head. The head considered is that of the first stage , obtained approximately by dividing total pump head by the number of stages. Taking 3% of total head would give a far more lenient — and wrong — result. If the pump is dismantled to correct its NPSH-r, that calls for a retest .

Some standards specify that the pump be dismantled after the shop running test, generally to inspect the bearings and mechanical seal. However, if the pump has performed satisfactorily during the shop test, dismantling can be skipped . Dismantling after test is required only in special circumstances: inconsistent test results; abnormal noise; higher-than-expected vibration; a prototype design. What the shop test actually buys you Reviewing hydraulic and mechanical performance by shop test ensures there are no unexpected deviations or ambiguity about performance after installation and commissioning. More practically: once the performance curve has been established at the shop test, that curve tends to remain consistent for the life of the machine so long as there is no mechanical damage or wear. So when a commissioning anomaly appears and the pump has not been dismantled or mechanically altered, the shop test curve is your evidence that the discrepancy lies in the system layout or system components — not the pump. That is exactly the argument you need in a commissioning dispute, and you only have it if the test was done and documented properly. See Chapter 08 . Correct and accurate pump specification, inspection and testing are the building blocks of reliable operation. The next block is installation.

Siting, foundation design, grouting, alignment, suction and discharge piping rules, pre-operational checks and the start-up sequence — the stage where most of a pump's service life is won or lost. After specification, selection, sizing, inspection and testing, installation is the next key factor in reliable operation. Properly installed, operated and maintained, a pump can give many years of trouble-free service. Incorrectly installed, maintenance and operational problems will impede its performance for its entire life — and no amount of later maintenance recovers what a bad installation costs. Installation needs careful preparation and planning, coordinated between the supervising engineer, the mechanical and electrical contractors, and the suppliers. It is a series of steps, and each one has to be right before the next begins. Site location A pre-installation activity. Before the equipment even arrives, layout drawings are available, which allows the site location to be selected and marked out. Ergonomics is a prime factor. Where equipment is accessible for maintenance, technici

A pre-installation activity. Before the equipment even arrives, layout drawings are available, which allows the site location to be selected and marked out. Ergonomics is a prime factor. Where equipment is accessible for maintenance, technicians perform better and operators activate and control it more efficiently. A pump or motor that is difficult to access and maintain becomes a cause of longer downtime and lower availability. Poor workmanship caused by difficult access leads directly to lower reliability. Safety is the main aspect A difficult site has a higher probability of accidents. Site selection deserves considerable attention and should be done by someone with real practical experience in pump operation and maintenance — not solely from a layout drawing.

Examine all pumps and auxiliary equipment on receipt for signs of apparent damage, and notify any damage found. Where installation is not immediate, store in a clean, dry location protected from damage, following the manufacturer's recommendations and protecting from environmental extremes. Check the equipment before storage to anticipate problems at installation time — check sizes, the design features called for on the plans and specifications, and all interface components. These simple early checks minimise installation problems considerably. Recommended practices on receipt and in storage Openings Keep all nozzles and openings covered or plugged until the piping is attached. Bearings Fill bearing housings with oil of the recommended viscosity. For greased bearings, pump in new grease and displace the old. Preservation Coat all exposed surfaces with rust preventive. For storage beyond 6 months , coat the internals too with a suitable rust preventive or oil mist. Packing Remove pump packings with sleeves. Mechanical seals Handle carefully. Do not subject to impact or excessive vibration.

If installing immediately after receipt, carry out an alignment check of the pump with its motor on the baseplate , to confirm that the final alignment tolerances in the specification are actually achievable. Use a reverse dial indicator or laser alignment method. Why do this before anything is grouted If the specified alignment is not achievable, there is still time to rectify the fault — which saves time and money and prevents the quick fixes that get applied when the problem is discovered at the final stage of installation. Once correct alignment is confirmed, the pump and motor can be removed from the base to ease installation and prevent damage to critical components.

Once the site location is fixed, locating the foundation is largely fine-tuning to bring it into line with existing equipment, piping and vessels. The site-location factors still apply: allow room for walkways, existing and new piping, operator and technician accessibility, and aesthetics. What can usually be altered is the orientation of the pump's face, its proximity to walls, and the height and depth of the foundation. Changing pump height changes the hydraulics If pump height or location is altered, ensure the operating parameters can still be met — and the prime consideration is the NPSH margin or ratio . Raising a pump 600 mm to clear a walkway can quietly consume the whole suction margin. Where installation standards or guidelines already exist, obtain the responsible engineer's consent.

The foundation has two specific purposes: to support the pump so it operates safely; its mass damps the pump vibrations. It must provide enough rigidity to absorb the axial, transverse and torsional loads the rotating pump imposes. Proper structural design requires an evaluation of soil conditions so that both dynamic and static forces are considered. Foundation design requirements Mass At least three times the total weight of supported equipment. Isolation Rests on solid or stabilised earth, completely independent of other foundations, pads, walls or operating platforms. Concrete A minimum of 3000 psi steel-reinforced concrete. Resonance Resonant frequency must not be excitable by pump operating speed or multiples of it. Common base All units — pump, gearbox and motor — rest on a common foundation . Thermal Designed for uniform temperatures , to minimise distortion and misalignment. Seismic Designed accounting for regional seismic activity. Rules of thumb for dimensions The 30° rule. Drop two lines from the pump centre at 30° to the vertical. The width of the foundation should exceed their spread . Mass. Foundation weight at least three times the mass of supported equipment. Edge margin. For pumps under 500 hp, at least 3 in between baseplate edge and foundation edge, all the way around. For higher horsepower, 6 in .

With location, orientation and dimensions fixed, mark the location and excavate a correctly sized cavity to the correct depth. Typical requirements: cement saw, jackhammer, air supply, wheelbarrow, shovels, a small front-end loader, a disposal method for excavated material, and digging permits. Excavation for an average-sized centrifugal pump takes a maximum of about two days. Then place the forms — reusable or single use. The forms must be true, solid, well braced and liquid-tight . Leak tightness matters particularly because epoxies seep through small holes far more readily than cement . Once installed, ensure the forms are level, square and securely fastened to the floor or ground — the weight of cement and epoxy bears on them and can easily cause a shift. If the form shifts during pouring, the job has to be terminated and restarted. For epoxy pours, coat the insides of the forms with an anti-stick material so the forms can be removed without destroying them. Wax is a good anti-stick material: it coats well and the forms can be coated before assembly and installation.

Install the rebar and pump hold-down bolts. Rebar ring and post count depends on the foundation dimensions — a 60″ × 60″ × 36″ foundation typically takes three rings of rebar tied to eight posts . Rebar is placed several inches from the sides, top and bottom, equally spaced from top and bottom. Then the anchor bolts. Length is typically 10 to 15 times the bolt diameter , which is what gives the bolt enough stretch to develop the design holding force. The anchor bolt failure nobody expects If epoxy grout is allowed to grip the anchor bolt, the bolt will break at the grout surface even when tightened only to the design torque — because it cannot stretch. This requirement is met at foundation design stage by using bolt sleeves in the concrete. Where sleeves are used, fill them with non-binding material — sand, flexible foam or wax — to prevent epoxy bonding to the bolt. The exposed length from the top of the concrete to the bottom of the baseplate can also be wrapped with one layer of weather stripping and one layer of duct tape. Typical ANSI pump anchor bolt detail An acceptable hold-down bolt for most ANSI pumps is a 5/8 in J-bolt mounted in a 1½ in pipe , the pipe at least 6 in long: the J-bolt extends past the top of the pipe by at least the pump base height plus 1½ in; it extends past the bottom of the pipe by an inch or two before the "J" bends; a washer is welded to the bot

Pour the concrete mix slowly while stirring the cement — normally from a cement truck, or pumped or wheelbarrowed where a truck cannot reach. Trowel-finish the top of the pad when the cement is ready. Curing must complete before epoxy grout The epoxy–concrete bond is sensitive to moisture , which must be prevented at all times. Curing of freshly poured concrete must complete before epoxy grout is applied. Proper method: run the ASTM 157-80 concrete shrinkage test to determine when shrinkage drops to minimum — that indicates the end of the chemical reaction between cement and water. Rule of thumb in its absence: standard concrete (5-bag mix) — 28 days ; quick-setting concrete (6–7 bag mix) — 7 days . Field check: tape one square foot of plastic sheet over the concrete block and leave overnight. Moisture on the underside means the concrete is not ready. Repeat until no moisture appears. Removing laitance Surface preparation begins two to three days after the pour. It may be necessary to chip the top ½″ to 1″ from the foundation surface to remove the cement-rich surface layer called laitance — a weak surface created when concrete is cast, which would not provide proper adhesion or support for the grout beneath the baseplate. Sand blasting removes laitance and exposes the aggregate. The most common method is to wait for the concrete to cure and then chip the laitance with light-dut

It is sometimes necessary or advantageous to make the entire foundation from epoxy. Initial cost is higher, but it offers: superior vibration damping; better chemical resistance; faster curing — epoxy cures in 24 hours , against 7 days minimum even for quick-setting cement, so equipment installation can begin almost immediately. Procedure: mix epoxy parts A (resin) and B (hardener) per instructions. Mix both parts completely and leave nothing unmixed — unmixed parts are a hazard needing special disposal, whereas the mixture of the two is not hazardous. Add the mixed resin to an empty mortar mixer, then add the aggregate: pure silica , some with sand texture and some with pea-gravel texture, at a specific ratio set by ambient conditions. Pure silica is used instead of sand and pea gravel for its superior heat-sink capability , and it adds to the overall strength. Mix to uniform consistency, slowly, so no air is entrained — air is detrimental to pour strength. A spiral-blade mortar mixer is best suited. Pour into the hole and repeat until complete. An average-size foundation can be poured in under 4 hours when properly administered. Complete any finishing touches before the epoxy cures.

Remove all equipment from the baseplate or sole plate before grouting. This helps level the plate and reduces unwanted distortion. The pump and motor/turbine/engine are mounted after the baseplate has been properly grouted. Baseplate preparation checklist Grout-contact surface Coat with inorganic zinc silicate or a compatible primer. The surface should be bare or rusted, free of blisters, and not smooth — a smooth surface will not bond properly with epoxy grout. Grout openings At least one grouting opening in each bulkhead section and/or each 12 ft² of base area as a minimum. Vent holes At the corners of each bulkhead compartment , to ensure no voids form from trapped air. Typically ½ in diameter. Corners Round all baseplate corners to 20 in radius . Epoxy shrinks as it cures; rounding prevents stress corrosion in the grout. Sharp corners eventually crack the grout. Cleanliness Free from oil, grease and rust before placing on the foundation.

Rest the baseplate on the foundation supported on levelling screws, rectangular levelling shims or taper wedges placed close to the foundation bolts to prevent distortion. Coat levelling screws adequately with grease or wax to prevent epoxy adhesion. Baseplate level tolerance 0.002 in per foot Min. shim under driver 1/8 in Machined surface overhang 0.1 in beyond feet Level side-to-side, end-to-end and diagonally to within 0.002 in per foot. Machined surfaces must be flat and parallel, and the mounting surface tolerance must remain the same after the anchor bolts are tightened . Once level, confirm all wedges and shims are in contact with both baseplate and foundation, tighten the foundation bolts evenly, and re-check the levels . Before the grout is poured — four things that are hard to fix later Check the elevation of the machined surfaces to confirm it allows a minimum 1/8 in shim thickness under the driving equipment . Ensure eight alignment positioning screws are provided for positioning the driver. Machined mounting surfaces should extend 0.1 in beyond the pump and driver feet on all sides . Drill and tap two holes on the baseplate flanges each side of the anchor-bolt holes to make provision for 1½ in jack/levelling screws. Grease and insert the coupling guard bolts into the baseplate. It is difficult to drill and tap those holes once they are filled with epoxy grout.

Grout is a hardenable material — mortar, concrete or epoxy — placed under and around the baseplate to ensure intimate contact with the foundation. The reasons for grouting: to provide a uniformly distributed load-bearing surface ; to provide effective damping of machinery vibration; to fill cavities and cover projections, eliminating unsafe conditions and improving performance. Two types are in use: epoxy grout (resin, hardener and aggregate), and cement plus a natural or metallic aggregate .

Forms. Lay out heavy-duty forms — epoxy weighs nearly 2.5 times as much as concrete . Use ¾ in plywood with adequate bracing. Wax-coat the surfaces that will contact the epoxy, normally three coats with sufficient interval between coats for wax penetration and drying. Give the forms a 1 in, 45° chamfer on the vertical and horizontal edges so mating allows minimum seepage; use a plastic sealant at all joints and at the foundation interface if needed. One pour or two. API-design baseplates require two-pour grouts: one to fill the void between concrete and baseplate flanges, and one to fill the void between the baseplate flange and the top of the baseplate. However, if the free surface of the grout at the baseplate flanges is confined 6–7 in higher, the grout level at the top of the baseplate can be filled in one pour . A one-pour grout can be accomplished in 45 minutes and, with curing complete in 24 hours, the forms can be removed — and where ambient temperature is above 25 °C, the pump and driver can be installed as soon as the forms come off. A two-pour job needs more time and cost. Temperature window. Epoxy grouts have a narrow range for mixing and placement: 10 °C to 35 °C for best life, flowability and curing. Below that, add low-temperature accelerators and keep the foundation and baseplate heated. Above it, place temporary shades over the baseplate 24 hours before and 48

The procedure is similar to epoxy. Lay out the forms with the same precautions. Where the foundation is concrete, keep the top surface saturated with water for the period recommended by the grout manufacturer, then remove that water from the top and from boltholes just before placing the grout . Prevent grout entering the anchor bolt sleeves: fill sleeves with a non-bonding pliable material such as asphalt or silicone rubber moulding compound , to prevent a water pocket around the bolt. Wrap duct tape around the exposed anchor bolt threads to prevent direct grout contact. Temperature requirements are similar to epoxy, but the range must be maintained for a minimum of 24 hours after pouring . Prepare the grout per instructions with the right amount and quality of oil-free water . Placement must be rapid and continuous. Start at one end of the baseplate and work toward the other, to ensure all air is positively vented and no pockets are trapped. Cement grout finishing levels Grout cut back To the bottom outer edge of the baseplate or sole plate, tapered to the existing concrete. Flange-type support baseplates Top of grout at the top of the flange . Solid-sided baseplates and sole plates Top of grout 1 in above the bottom of the baseplate or underside of the sole plate. Outside top edges Chamfered at 45° . After initial set, trim to the levels shown on the drawings. After complete

Once the grout is cured and the base is clean, remove the bolts used to seal the boltholes and install the pump — which should be in operation-ready condition when it goes on the base. Place the driver, motor or turbine, at the location shown on the drawings and confirm the distance between shaft ends (DBSE) : set DBSE with the pump and driver shafts pulled toward each other ; for motor drives with sleeve bearings , set DBSE with the motor shaft at its magnetic centre . Check rotation before coupling up For an electric motor, confirm the motor is wired correctly for the correct direction of rotation. This check must be carried out before the equipment is coupled up. Pumps, seals and magnetic drive bearings can be ruined if operated dry or in reverse. After the rotation check, de-energise the motor and lock out the breaker .

Align pump and motor to the final tolerances using a reverse dial gauge or a laser alignment tool. Soft foot This is the stage at which a soft foot condition manifests. Loosen the hold-down bolts one at a time and use a dial gauge to record movement between the machine foot and the baseplate or sole plate. Soft foot limit 0.025 mm (1 mil) Any movement in excess of 1 mil indicates soft foot and must be corrected by adding the required amount of shims under the feet. Thermal growth with a steam turbine driver Alignment with a steam turbine is usually carried out at ambient conditions. When steam is introduced the turbine centreline rises, producing misalignment. Compute the vertical growth and offset for it: Rise = 1.2 mils per inch of height from base to centreline, per 100 °C rise (equivalently 1.2 mm per metre of height, per 100 °C rise) Example: an impulse steam turbine with 130 °C exhaust in a 30 °C ambient is a 100 °C rise. With 12 in from foot base to shaft centreline, the thermal growth is 14.4 mils .

t: Then bolt the piping — and re-check
b: After alignment is complete, bolt up the piping associated with the pump and steam turbine. Then check the alignment again ; it should give similar readings. This is the check that catches pipe strain If the alignment readings have changed after bolting the piping, investigate the piping and make suitable corrections . Left unattended, this causes stress on the pump casing and nozzles — and it is the root cause behind a great many "unexplained" bearing and seal failures months later. Once alignment is approved, drill the support pads for the pumps and drivers at two locations for taper dowels. Locate the dowels preferably at the end carrying the thrust bearings .

Piping associated with the pump must be anchored and supported independently of the pump . Without adequate anchorage, expansion and contraction of the line transfers forces to the pump casing. Where pipes are not supported, their weight is borne by the pump casing and nozzles, causing them to deflect and crack — and the pump's seal life suffers from the same strain. Connections must be carefully aligned axially, angularly and in length , and the flange boltholes must be in phase with the pump nozzle holes. The one-minute test for pipe strain Disconnect all the suction and discharge flanges on the pump. If levers are required to force the pipe flange onto the pump nozzles to facilitate bolting, you can be certain the pump will sooner or later start giving bearing and other problems. This is the single most valuable check in this chapter. It costs nothing and it finds the defect that no amount of subsequent alignment, balancing or bearing replacement will cure.

Suction piping rules Support Piping run and connection fittings properly aligned and supported separately to reduce strain on the casing. Straight run Straight run leading to the suction nozzle at least 3 to 6 pipe diameters from the upstream elbow. Elbow type Standard type or long radius . Negative suction All suction piping must be airtight . Pipe size At least one commercial size larger than the pump inlet opening. Reducer Eccentric reducer with the flat side on top — so air cannot be trapped in the line. Straight length after the eccentric reducer: 2 pipe diameters . Velocity Sized so liquid velocity is not more than 2 to 3 m/s . Slope In negative suction, a continuous rise to the suction inlet ; minimum slope 6 mm per 100 mm . Not required in flooded suction. Isolation valves In negative suction, no isolation valves recommended ; they may be provided in flooded suction. Even fully open, a valve contributes friction loss and lowers available NPSH — and on a pump with high negative suction lift, NPSH-a is already low. Drain and gauge Provide a means to drain the contents between the suction isolation valves and the pump casing , and a tapping for a suction pressure gauge . Sump, submergence and vortexing Submergence and strainer geometry in negative suction Strainer submergence Minimum depth at least 3 pipe diameters , measured from the upper row of holes of the strainer. St

Piping run and fittings properly aligned and supported separately . Discharge pipe size at least one commercial size larger than the pump outlet. Minimise the number of fittings and size changes to prevent fluid friction losses. Check valve of the non-slam type , to prevent hydraulic shock. Isolation valve downstream of the check valve , so the check valve can be taken out for servicing. Concentric reducers in the discharge, to minimise friction loss. (Contrast the suction, which takes an eccentric reducer.) A pressure tapping as close as possible to the pump outlet and before the isolation valve , to measure shut-off head. A second pressure tapping downstream of the reducer , as a good indicator of operating pressure. Expansion joints only after careful piping analysis , especially where discharge pressures are high.

Once the shop tests are witnessed and verified, the pump is disconnected and transported to site for installation and commissioning. Expect the duty point to differ — and know why Once installed, checked, primed and tested, the pump may or may not operate at the design point as calculated. There are several legitimate reasons: "As designed" versus "as constructed." Differences in pipe runs, number of bends, or quality of fittings change the frictional resistance the pump must overcome — up or down — moving the operating point away from the design point. Over-generous friction allowance at design stage. Too much allowance for H f means the pump selected is oversized , and it will operate off the performance curve or far to the right of BEP. Change in fluid properties. Anomalies introduced between shop test and site — wrong impeller size, wrong pump speed, incorrect direction of rotation. Commissioning acceptance of the system resistance evaluation Measured deviation from design point Verdict on the total system resistance H ts Within ±2.5% Good The evaluation of H ts is considered good. Within ±5% Satisfactory The evaluation is considered satisfactory. Greater than 5% Investigate The system needs to be checked out. It is always good practice to have the pump manufacturer's representative involved at installation, testing and commissioning. Commissioning test logs , similar to th

Mainly focused on the auxiliary systems. Pre-operational checklist Double mechanical seals (back-to-back, external pressurised sealant) Flush and clean the lines before connecting them to the pump. If the casing is pressurised, check the sealant supply pressure is 1–1.5 kg/cm² above casing pressure — lower pressure can cause the inner seal to open up and contaminate the process fluid. Tandem mechanical seals The overhead reservoir providing thermosyphon circulation for the outboard seal must be thoroughly cleaned by oil flush before connecting to the pump. Cooling water Flush all cooling water lines to pumps and turbines. Confirm supply and return lines are connected to the correct headers. Bearing lubrication Drain bearing housings of their oil and refill with fresh oil of correct viscosity . Verify oil reaches all bearings. Oil mist systems Must be up and running for almost 12 hours before start-up . Oil mist piping must slope toward the equipment with no sags or low spots. Re-confirm Direction of rotation of the motor · over-speed trip setting of a steam turbine · greasing of the coupling · earthing of equipment . Separate lube oil system Where the pump and turbine have one, all alarms and trips must be checked and tested . Final mechanical Rotate the pump by hand and look for any rubs. Place the coupling guard and tighten the bolts. Electrical Inform the electrical departme

The sequence from here: Open the pump suction valve slowly and check all joints for leakage. Open the pump casing to vent any vapour . This can be tricky with flashing hydrocarbons, so it has to be done several times. If the pumping temperature is high, allow the pump to warm up . For multistage pumps with long rotors, it is a good idea to keep rotating the rotor 180° every 30 minutes while warming — otherwise the rotor sags and bows. Open the sealant and cooling water lines and ensure circulation . Discharge valve position depends on the pump type : kept closed for low specific speed pumps, open for higher specific speed pumps. This prevents overloading the motor drive — see Chapter 05 . Confirm the electrical supply has been energised. Start the pump.

First-run checks and their acceptance Discharge pressure Check it is along expected lines. If the pressure does not come up, the most probable reason is improper priming — stop the pump and re-prime. On a low specific speed pump, the discharge pressure falls as the discharge valve is opened, which is normal. Flow rate Confirm. Vibration Take measurements of the entire train with a data collector. Record overall and filtered readings, and record and store the frequency plots . Study them for possible defects. Because overall vibration varies with the operating point, record readings and frequency plots at 4 or 5 operating points including the normal and rated points — this is your vibration baseline for the life of the machine. Seal leakage Confirm. Some leakage in the initial stages is possible and may settle down after wear-in. Bearing temperature Pump and motor/turbine bearings no more than 10–20 °C above ambient . Higher indicates a bearing in distress — unless they are greased, in which case the most probable cause is over-greasing . A vibration or shock pulse analysis confirms it; if so, wait 24 hours and allow the excess grease to work out. Performance check Once steady state is achieved, carry out a performance check and determine the efficiency. Plot it on the pump characteristic curves — this is the commissioning baseline for all future performance monitoring . Shutdow

Condition monitoring and overhaul: the four-pillar predictive programme, failure diagnosis before strip-down, the dimensional checks that matter, reassembly of single-stage, vertical and multistage pumps, and the economics of when to overhaul. The basis of centrifugal pump maintenance is a direct function of criticality. A garden water pump does not require the attention of a boiler feed water pump in a power plant or a firewater pump in a refinery. So the first task is not technical — it is to classify the machine. Criticality and maintenance philosophy A pump is critical where: failure can affect plant safety; it is essential for plant operation and a shutdown will curtail process throughput; there is no standby or installed spare ; it is a large horsepower pump; capital cost is high and it is expensive to repair, or has a long repair lead time; it is a perennial "bad actor" — a pump that wrecks on the slightest provocation of an off-duty operation; it is part of a pump train where better operation could save energy or improve yields. Classification and the maintenance philosophy that follows Class Maintenance philosophy Cri

A pump is critical where: failure can affect plant safety; it is essential for plant operation and a shutdown will curtail process throughput; there is no standby or installed spare ; it is a large horsepower pump; capital cost is high and it is expensive to repair, or has a long repair lead time; it is a perennial "bad actor" — a pump that wrecks on the slightest provocation of an off-duty operation; it is part of a pump train where better operation could save energy or improve yields. Classification and the maintenance philosophy that follows Class Maintenance philosophy Critical Predictive and proactive techniques Essential Preventive maintenance General purpose Less stringent — may be run to failure In practice a mix-and-match of techniques is applied, with the prime intention of maximising runtime lengths and reducing downtime and costs. Current focus for continuous process plant pumps is a blend of Predictive and Preventive Maintenance (PPM) . The four pillars of a PPM programme Individually each gives an indication of pump condition. Collectively they give the complete picture. Running only one or two is the commonest reason condition monitoring programmes fail to predict anything. Performance monitoring Vibration monitoring Oil and particle analysis System analysis — the one most often omitted

Six parameters tell you how the pump is performing: suction pressure, P s discharge pressure, P d flow, Q pump speed, N pump efficiency, η power With an electric motor driver, power is the easiest to measure with portable instruments clipped onto the phase cables, giving amps, volts, power factor and hence power. Combined with the process parameters, efficiency can be computed and benchmarked against the OEM's expected values — see the procedure in Chapter 03 . Suction and discharge pressures are measured using calibrated pressure gauges screwed onto the fittings provided on the pipelines with isolation valves.

Normally done with obtrusive instruments — venturi tubes, orifice plates, pitot tubes. Where none are installed, non-obtrusive doppler or transit-time devices can be used, and these can be portable. Caution on clamp-on flow meters Each device must be calibrated , and independent testing has shown these devices are sensitive to the liquid being pumped and are not precisely accurate . Treat a clamp-on reading as an indication, and be careful about declaring a pump degraded on its evidence alone. Analysis of efficiency — or inefficiency — helps determine whether the losses are hydraulic , internal recirculation , or mechanical .

Direct-reading thermodynamic pump efficiency monitors (the Yates meter and similar) interpret operating efficiency dynamically by measuring and computing the temperature rise of the fluid — in millikelvin — as it moves from suction to discharge. Highly sensitive temperature probes and pressure transducers are positioned on the suction and discharge pipework, while a power meter provides the power absorbed by the motor. Motor efficiency from the motor manufacturer and drive losses are factored into the software, which then calculates pump operating efficiency. That reading is compared against the commissioning data to determine the drop in performance. Advantages of thermodynamic monitoring No dismantling of the pump is necessary. Cost and energy savings by increasing pump availability and reliability. Maintenance timing can be predicted and planned accurately , in line with predictive and planned strategies. Where a flow meter is installed, the monitor can verify the accuracy of the meter by calculating Q from the empirical power relationship. Capital cost is high, but return on investment may be realised quickly on large-capacity systems with numerous pumps. Alternatively the service can be purchased, or a provider contracted to measure and report periodically as part of the PPM programme.

Online or offline depending on criticality. Online measurement uses proximity probes to measure shaft vibration. The most common form is offline using portable data collectors measuring casing vibration. Vibration is measured for both the pump and its driver , at the bearing locations. Reporting requires a convention for labelling bearings, and the general convention is to start labelling from where the power comes in : Bearing labelling convention for a motor-driven pump Label Location A Motor non-drive end bearing B Motor drive end bearing C Pump outboard bearing (next to the coupling) D Pump inboard bearing (away from the coupling) Take vibrations in three Cartesian directions — vertical, horizontal and axial — at each point. Machine construction is such that defects can show up in any of the three planes, so all three must be measured. Reporting is typically a 4 × 3 matrix: Example vibration report — velocity, mm/s peak Point Vertical Horizontal Axial A — motor NDE 2.4 1.7 1.0 B — motor DE 2.1 1.9 1.2 C — pump outboard 4.3 5.6 2.7 D — pump inboard 3.7 4.1 2.1

t: Sources of error in hand-held measurement
b: Hand-held measurements are subject to a number of errors, and personnel taking them must be aware of them. Errors arise from: position on the machine; probe angle ; probe type ; contact pressure . Interpretation requires a baseline, not a limit As established at commissioning , a base reading is taken at several operating points . Vibration levels are minimum at BEP and rise as the operating point moves away. Comparison against the original base readings is what indicates deterioration in mechanical health. In the absence of a baseline, the limits in API 610 can be used as a reference — but a trend against the machine's own baseline is far more diagnostic than an absolute number against a standard.

Frequency analysis determines the nature of the fault. The three most common problems associated with pumps are easily detected: Unbalance Misalignment Bearing defects Less frequent hydraulic problems can also be detected — cavitation , and improper impeller-to-volute-tongue gaps (which show at vane pass frequency ). Infrared thermography can be used alongside vibration analysis to pinpoint a problem source by detecting an elevated temperature at the trouble spot.

Testing the oil and the particles in it is a good indicator of both bearing condition and the quality of the company's oil programme. Several tests determine bearing condition, or determine why a bearing failed so that appropriate corrective action follows: spectrographic analysis; viscosity analysis; infrared analysis; total acid number; wear particle analysis and wear particle count; moisture content. Most of these must be performed under laboratory conditions, though portable instruments now allow some testing on site. Given that 0.002% water costs 48% of bearing life , the moisture content result alone justifies the programme.

System analysis determines the system resistance curve of the installed pump, which can then be used to evaluate NPSH-a in the as-installed condition. A typical system analysis includes NPSH-a, NPSH-r, static head, friction loss through the system, and a complete review of the piping configuration, valves and fittings. The pillar everyone skips, and the cost of skipping it System analysis is often overlooked because it is assumed the system was constructed and the pumps are operated in accordance with the design specification. This is often not the case. It is imperative to know where the pumps are being operated to perform a correct analysis — and that depends on the system. The process must also be understood, because it ultimately dictates how the pumps are operated. All indicators may show the pump in distress when the real problem is that it is being run at low or high flow, with excessive hydraulic forces inside it. Overhaul that pump and it will come back in six months, because nothing about the cause was addressed.

Pump maintenance is not primarily about dismantling and assembling pumps. It is an activity to prolong the efficient runtimes of the equipment and improve its overall effectiveness. The techniques above monitor health and, on indication of distress, indicate the cause and severity. If a pump is in distress it should be taken up for corrective action immediately — prolonging maintenance lets primary failures cascade into secondary failures, increasing both downtime and cost. For non-essential pumps it may be acceptable to leave the machine unmonitored until failure. The definition that changes how you manage pumps "Failure" does not necessarily mean a seizure or a seal blowout forcing a shutdown. A pump is installed to perform a function under specified conditions. When it is no longer capable of performing that function under those conditions, it has failed. So if a pump must deliver a certain flow at a certain horsepower, and horsepower consumption exceeds the specified limit, the pump has failed — even though it may be running perfectly smoothly. That reframing is what converts energy monitoring from a nice-to-have into a failure detection method.

Typical failure causes in real applications: mechanical seal failure; excessive vibration; pump rubbing or seizure; inadequate performance — flow, head or power consumption; leaking casing. Diagnose before you dismantle Before a pump is removed, establish the failure type . Once it is in pieces on the workshop floor, the evidence of why is largely gone.

Check with the operating crew on the perceived cause of failure . If it is safe to operate the pump, re-run it to diagnose the failure by: sight, smell, noise and touch ; vibration analysis; bearing temperature measurement; a performance check. These steps indicate the probable cause and — critically — establish whether it is specific to the pump or to the process or pumping system , including the suction and discharge systems.

t: Field checks if the problem is the pump
b: Pre-removal field check sequence 1 Check flush and quench lines for leak, corrosion or plugging 2 Check the balance line, if the design includes one 3 Check the suction strainer for blockage and ensure all valves are open 4 Visually check the oil condition and the oil level 5 Check the coupling for wear or lack of grease 6 Check the condition of the gauges 7 Observe the condition of the baseplate and pump supports 8 Isolate and danger-tag the pump valves and motor (padlock the motor switch) 9 While dismantling, notice the pipe strain on the pump 10 Once decoupled, measure the radial and end clearance of both pump and motor 11 Run the motor and confirm satisfactory operation. If unsatisfactory, remove the motor for repair too.

Once the pump is out for overhaul, the observation process does not end — it becomes more focused. Match and mark all parts before dismantling. Open the casing bolts and separate the casing or volute. Inspect the casing for corrosion and erosion. Inspect the gasket face particularly, to ensure sufficient land area and a smooth surface; repair appropriately if damaged. Inspect the impeller and nut for wear, corrosion and erosion. Inspect the vanes for pitting or cavities in the regions identified in Chapter 03 — this distinguishes cavitation from suction or discharge recirculation, and that distinction determines whether the fix is hydraulic or operational. Inspect the impeller and casing wear rings for signs of rub or detachment. A rub indicates excessive shaft deflection, improper assembly, or piping strain . Open the seal flange nuts and check the seal tension . Remove the impeller after opening the nut. Where it has balancing holes, unplug them. Inspect the backside wear rings carefully. Pull the shaft sleeve out together with the rotary head of the seal. Dismantle carefully and check for wear signs on the primary seal face and on the secondary seals — O-rings and gaskets. Check the bearings for roughness and measure the endplay.

t: The dimensional checks that decide the overhaul
b: Strip-down measurements, methods and limits Check Method Limit What exceeding it means Endplay / axial float Dial gauge pointer against any step on the shaft, magnetic base on the seal housing. Bump the shaft to one end, zero the gauge, move to the other end, read. 0.001–0.003 in (0.02–0.07 mm) Higher float causes pitting and fretting at the contact points in the packing or mechanical seal area. Establish whether the cause is improper bearing assembly in the housing or defective bearings. Shaft runout Shaft on V-blocks on a flat machinist's table, dial gauge at various locations, rotate by hand. Alternatively clamp at lathe centres, zero on the journals and read elsewhere. A third method — dial gauge fixed to the housing with the pointer on the shaft OD — is only valid if the pump bearings are in good condition . 0.05 mm max (target ≤ 0.025 mm) Shaft roundness combined with a permanent bow. Greatest effect is on the mechanical seal : a 3 mil (0.075 mm) runout moves the seal faces 3 mil per side — 6 mil total . A bent shaft also causes vibration with a large impact on seal and bearing life. Straighten if higher. With a sleeve fitted, measure on the sleeve OD; combined runout of shaft and sleeve must be within 0.05 mm , so hold each to 0.025 mm. Shaft radial movement Dial gauge fixed to the housing as close as possible to the inboard bearing housing, pointer on the shaft OD. Lift

Where bearings feel rough or there is excessive radial and axial float, dismantle the bearing housing to replace them. Normally the outer race has a transition fit with the housing and the inner races have an interference fit on the shaft , so the shaft with bearings can be drawn out of the housing with a slight tap. Bearings are removed from the shaft using a hydraulic press . Once the bearings are off, measure the bore and shaft OD dimensions and work out the bearing fits. Check the shaft for straightness at this point — with the shaft bare, the V-block method is available — then polish and keep it ready for reassembly. Repairing excessive bearing fits Housings can be re-sleeved with rings of the same material . Shaft diameters can be subjected to weld build-up and re-machining — but this must consider the material of construction and the section thickness. Some materials need heat treatment, and a smaller-diameter shaft can warp if the weld procedure produces excessive heat build-up. Do not treat a weld repair on a small shaft as routine.

The impeller is a rotating part subject to high velocity, and the adverse effects of poor hydraulic design show up as wear and erosion. Examine the vanes for cavitation and recirculation evidence — and communicate this information to operations , because the cause is in how the pump is being run. Treat any corrosion of the impeller seriously and review the material of construction if corrosion rates are excessive. A badly worn or corroded impeller should be replaced. Where the impeller is to be reused, check the fit of its bore with the shaft, and its keyway. Wear ring clearance — the highest-leverage measurement in the overhaul Measure the wear ring diameter and compare with its mating ring in the casing. Clearances must be in line with the API 610 recommendations . Where restoring clearance pays best Wear ring clearance is probably the single factor with the greatest impact on pump efficiency — higher clearance means higher recirculation loss. And the percentage power loss from wear clearances is much higher in low specific speed pumps . Experimental data on double-suction pumps shows leakage losses as a percentage of power input falling steeply as specific speed rises. So restoring clearances on low specific speed pumps gives the highest return in leakage loss reduction. Those pumps deserve the most attention on wear ring clearance. (After Karassik, When To Maintain Centrifu

Measure and record all fits of the casing and mating parts. Remove, clean, inspect and refit all plugs and fittings. Mounting pads must be flat and parallel to the pump centreline. Clean the casing and polish the gasket area with emery paper so no old gasket material adheres. Internal coating — a genuine efficiency recovery Where there are signs of corrosion or wear, consider coating the internals with a resistant epoxy or equivalent. The procedure: Descale the internals by ash, sand or grit blasting. For salt water applications, steam clean first to ensure all salt contamination is removed, then grit blast again. Apply the final epoxy coating. Why this is worth doing Such coatings smooth the surface roughness of the liquid path and so reduce hydraulic losses inside the pump. The reported impact on efficiency can be as high as 10–15% on a badly pitted casing. Few overhaul activities return that much. Clean the casing bolts, arrange the correct number, and coat with anti-seize compound.

Cleanliness of the seal and bearing housings is of utmost importance — it has a large impact on the life of the bearings and seals. Where the seal housing has cooling water jackets, get them chemically cleaned periodically . Inspect and check the bearing housing mating faces with the seal housing for proper fit. Check the bearing housing cover faces for smooth surface finish. Replace the oil seals or any other shaft seal. Check the concentricity of the bearing housing bores — place the housing on a horizontal boring machine with the dial gauge on the boring bar and measure in the vertical and horizontal planes. Alternatively use a dummy shaft with zero clearance in the housing bore. Paint the internals of the housing with oil-resistant paint. Bearing housings are typically cast iron, and in high-humidity, high-rainfall areas the inner surface corrodes. Corrosion dust washed around by the splashing oil acts as an abrasive for the bearings. Inspect the paint condition before assembly. Seal the housing against moisture ingress — install the bearing covers with proper bearing isolators . Clean the oil level gauge opening and fit a new gauge. Remove, clean and refit the bearing housing vent.

Check for straightness, thread condition at the impeller nut location, keyway fit at impeller and coupling locations, and fits for the anti-friction bearings. Dress up or repair rounded shoulders and steps. Inspect the lip seal area; if damaged, repair it or compensate with a sleeve of appropriate size.

Mechanical seals are the prime cause of pump failure. Efforts to improve seal reliability led to the standard API 682 , which recommends the use of cartridge seals . Cartridge seals eliminate the skilled workmanship required to assemble a seal at the user's end — which is exactly where seal assembly errors occur. Pump shaft sleeve Seal assembly preparation begins with the sleeve condition. The sleeve area under secondary seals such as O-rings or PTFE wedges is most prone to fretting . To eliminate the problem, that area can be plasma sprayed with a hard ceramic coating — chromium oxide, tungsten carbide or aluminium oxide — giving nearly 70 HRc , then ground to the exact dimension. Seal faces and flatness Seal faces should be renewed. Check the faces for flatness using an interferometer and optical flat : a monochromatic light source (helium or sodium) illuminates the piece through an optical flat placed on it, and the light reflects back through the flat producing interference light bands . Reading flatness from helium light bands Light bands Deviation 1 0.00029 mm (0.3 µm) 2 0.00059 mm 3 0.00088 mm (0.9 µm) Where the distance between optical flat and the measured piece is one-half the wavelength of helium, or an even multiple, the band shows black. That is a helium light band , measuring 0.3 microns (0.0000116 in). Concentric rings indicate the surface is neither concave nor

Leave new bearings packed until required for assembly. Confirm the housing fits with the bearing where there are repeated bearing failures or high bearing temperatures . Inspect the coupling for wear and its fit with the shaft; if normal, grease where applicable.

Preparation for assembly is a detailed exercise that lays the basis for a quick assembly and a reliable repair. It requires acceptable clearances and accurate data so that assembly is not hampered by incorrect dimensions or unclear expectations of a sub-assembly procedure. The consolidated chart is on the formula and data sheet .

Apply oil lightly on the bearing seat of the shaft. Shielding, if any, must face the proper direction. Angular contact bearings must also face the proper direction, and duplex bearings must be mounted with the proper faces together — arrangements vary from model to model, so refer to the OEM manual. Press the bearing on squarely — do not cock it onto the shaft. The sleeve used to press it on must be clean, cut square, and contact the inner race only . Press the bearing firmly against the shaft shoulder; the shoulder helps support and square the bearing. Where fits are tight, heat the bearings with an induction heater with a de-magnetising cycle . Temperature must not exceed 110 °C. Install the snap rings with the flat side against the bearing , and tighten the lock nuts. Lubricate the bearings. Wrap the assembly in plastic while the bearing housing is made ready. Before placing the rotor in the housing, ensure the housing is spotlessly clean . In pumps where the inboard bearing (closer to the impeller) is the locating (fixed) bearing, fix the bearing cover that provides the step to the outer race — after applying sealing compound to the mating faces . Smear oil on the bearing housing bores. Tap the shaft with mounted bearings into the housing until the outer race of the inboard bearing rests against the step. Apply sealing compound to the outboard mating face for the bearing co

Clamp the stationary seat firmly with the seals in the seal end plate. Bolt that to the seal housing. Slide the seal housing carefully over the shaft so there is no impact between the shaft surface and the stationary seat. Bolt it to the bearing housing, observing the match marks made before dismantling. This is necessary because if even a single bolthole is out of phase, it may be impossible to make the sealant connections in the field. Adjust the seal tension . The springs have a certain effect on face pressure, so a certain seal tension must be maintained. For multi-spring designs, seal tension is typically of the order of 3–4 mm depending on seal size; single-spring seals have a much higher seal tension. Seal tension = F − (S + A) = 3 mm with a gasket: Seal tension = F − (S + A + G) F free length of the assembled rotary head — from the edge of the sleeve to the seal face, without compression A distance between the shaft step and the face of the stationary seat (measured directly, or using a frame of reference based on the pump construction) S length of the sleeve — the difference between the easily measurable lengths L and M G gasket thickness, where the sleeve design uses a gasket rather than an O-ring to seal the shaft OD / sleeve ID gap Where seal tension is improper, cuts can be taken on the sleeve steps. Caution: ensure the step of the balance carbon and the sleeve ste

With the sleeve and rotary head in place, compression is achieved by installing the impeller and locking it to the shaft with the nut. After the impeller is fixed, measure the runout of the impeller wear ring in the installed condition — within 0.05 mm . Place the casing gasket in the pump casing. Bolt the casing to the seal housing flange, again observing the match marks . Tighten the bolts to the specified torque. Torque and anti-seize — the correction people forget Correct bolting torque depends on bolt size, thread and material — and critically on whether the bolt has been lubricated . If an anti-seize compound has been applied, the tightening torque must be set to approximately two-thirds of the torque specified for dry bolts. Apply anti-seize and then torque to the dry figure, and you have over-stressed every casing bolt.

Where the workshop can test seals, do it. Bolt blind flanges to the inlet and outlet nozzles. The blind flanges should be drilled and tapped for fittings to fill the pump with water and vent air from the topmost point. Fill with water and vent all air out. Pressurise to a minimum of 1–2 kg/cm² above the shut-off discharge pressure . Once pressurised, use compressed air to dry the pump externally , especially near the seal and shaft interface — otherwise you cannot tell a leak from residual water. Rotate the shaft slowly by hand and observe carefully for leaks from the seal. Examine the casing joint too. Investigate any drop in hydrotest pressure. If satisfactory, release the pressure and drain the water.

Mount the pump coupling half on the shaft. The shaft end should preferably be flush with the coupling half — but if it was not originally, that should have been recorded and kept to the same arrangement. Fit the sealant lines, oil level gauges, cooling water lines and any others. After removing the blind flanges, cover the pump nozzles completely with tape . The pump is ready for installation at site.

A vertical pump comprises: Head / driver assembly — an electric motor and a cast or fabricated base from which the column and bowl assembly is suspended; Column and shaft assembly — the column pipe links head assembly to bowl assembly and conducts the liquid from bowl to discharge. Inside it runs the pump shaft transmitting power from driver to impellers. The pumped liquid generally lubricates the line shaft bearings in the column. Pump bowl assembly — each bowl comprises impeller, suction and discharge casing. There are three reasons to overhaul a vertical turbine pump: Complete breakdown leading to unexpected disruption of a critical system. Reduced efficiency from increased clearances between bowls and enclosed impeller skirts, increased clearance between bowl shaft and bearings, and breakdown of the fluid passages. Over time, running a badly worn pump can be just as costly as some system shutdowns. Changed operational requirements in pressure and capacity. Why vertical pumps are harder A vertical pump has far more components than a horizontal pump, and its maintenance problems are different and substantially greater. The rotor is not stabilised by gravity and is prone to gyroscopic effects that can damage the rotor and the casing. Repair demands corresponding care.

The procedure is influenced by construction, and repair is much more complex than a single-stage pump. It is advisable to prepare a datasheet for the pump comprising all pump details, clearance and fits data, and any special remarks and procedures. Lay the pump horizontally on the floor with the discharge nozzle facing the ground. Take a paintbrush and match mark all the joints . Because bowl joints look similar, punch consecutive numbers on the joints — taking care these are not in addition to numbers from a previous overhaul, which would cause considerable confusion during assembly. Push the pump upper shaft toward the suction and measure the distance to the motor adapter face, and the adapter face configuration. Pull the rotor outward and re-measure that distance to get the total axial float of the rotor . Open the bowls. They may be individually screwed together, bolted with a series of bolts around the bowl flange (the most common design), or bolted with tie bolts extending from the bottom of the pumping section to the top through the bowls. Open one section at a time. Where a split collet bushing locks the impeller on the shaft, measure and record the distance between the shaft end and the impeller. Measure and record the float at each stage. As disassembly progresses, match mark the impellers, collets, keys, locking pins, split keeps and keeper plates , and arrange them

Bowl and impeller fluid passages Examine carefully for wear. A significant impact on efficiency results if they are damaged, pitted, have particle build-up, or have eroded coatings. Coatings are normally applied to the interior of the bowl assembly, mainly to enhance efficiency or protect internals — but fluid velocity and suspended solids often damage the coating. Cleaning, recoating or replacing the affected parts are options depending on severity. Shaft The bearing areas are susceptible to wear. If condition is good, measure the shaft runout: shaft on V-blocks or knife-edge rollers at the recommended distances, dial gauge at various locations, rotated a full circle by hand. Vertical pump shaft data Runout limit 3–4 mils (0.075–0.1 mm) . If higher, straighten within tolerance using a press. Construction A single-piece shaft is recommended whenever possible. If more than one piece is used and couplings are required, provide a radial weep hole in the centre of the coupling . Screw the shaft together and check runout. Material Bowl shaft typically a grade of stainless steel — 12% Cr steel, ASTM A581 / A582 , hot rolled bar, turned, ground and polished — rather than carbon steel, for abrasion and corrosion resistance. Abrasive service Shrunk-fitted sleeves in the wear areas, or chrome or other hard coatings at those locations. Lengths and straightness Shaft in lengths of 20–24 in

Assemble the pump in the vertical position. This prevents the risk of shaft or bowl assembly developing sag. Bowl bushing clearance is typically 9 mils and bowl spigot fits are 2–3 mils, so in a horizontal position it is bound to touch after 3–4 bowl assemblies . In the vertical position those clearances are distributed. Use the jack-bolt in the suction piece to position the end of the shaft and allow accurate spacing of the impellers. A load applied on previously installed impellers can knock them off their collet while installing the next one — and if impellers become loose, there is a grave danger of a rub on starting. Impellers fitted with collets need much more attention than those held by split rings, keys or snap rings. Excessive tightening of the collet can crack the impeller in the hub area. After the bowls are assembled, check the lift and rotate the rotor by hand to check for any internal rubbing. Where the pump is long, column sections have to be assembled horizontally. Rotate the assembled position 180° with the installation of every additional component — this staggers the alignment clearances and fits through the column length and keeps the assembly along the shaft centreline. After the columns are fitted, install the discharge head. At this stage, compare the shaft extension length against the figure taken before dismantling. Deviations of 1/16 to 1/8 in are nor

A barrel-type double case pump has two casings. The inner assembly comprises the complex shape of the stationary hydraulic passages; it sees the external differential pressure, so any bolting to hold it is minimal. It may be split axially into similar halves cast from the same pattern , or be of the multiple diffuser casing type. The outer casing acts as the pressure boundary for the pumped liquid and is designed as a pressure vessel. The rotor is either opposed impeller or in-line ; the latter has a balance disk to handle the much higher axial thrust. These pumps serve as boiler feed water pumps, charge pumps on high-temperature high-pressure hydrocarbons, water-flood pumps and pipeline pumps — all critical, all with expensive downtime. The spare inner assembly strategy Some designs have a fully separable inner case subassembly including the rotor , removable by taking off the outboard cover without breaking the suction line joint . Because downtime is expensive, a spare inner subassembly is usually made ready and held as a spare — during a repair the inner assemblies are simply swapped. For designs that include the journal and thrust bearing in the subassembly, downtime is reduced further because even those adjustments are made beforehand.

Shaft runout < 1 mil At bearing areas < 0.5 mil In some designs impellers are shrink fitted on the shaft to prevent mechanical looseness, positioned axially by split rings on the suction side of each impeller hub . The grooves for the split rings cause the shaft to develop runout, and because of the shrink fits the shaft fits must be measured and recorded . Next, balance the shaft with the half keys taped: mount on a balancing machine, spin to 300 rpm for about 10 minutes , measure shaft runout at mid-span and mark the angular position. Achieve balance by machining the face of the steps of the shaft , then re-check runout.

Place the shaft vertically . Stack all rotating components sequentially — impellers, thrust collar, balance drum if installed. Since most components are shrink fit, heat them to about 110–120 °C depending on bore and shaft diameters. Hold the match-marked split ring and key for the first-stage impeller in place. Mark the impeller keyway with a pen if it is blind at one end. Heat the impeller to 120 °C and slip it carefully over the key to position until it contacts the split rings. Apply constant downward pressure until the impeller has firmly gripped the shaft. To aid this, pass cooling air from the impeller OD to the suction eye until the impeller is at ambient. Install the other impellers the same way. Once all impellers are firmly fixed, measure rotor runout. If within limits, tighten the impeller nuts and re-check runout . If acceptable, fit all rotating components and send for balancing. If excessive runout is detected, the shaft nuts are the probable cause and their faces should be rectified. For the balancing procedure itself, see W. Edward Nelson, Monitoring Repairs to Your Pumps , 12th International Pump Users Symposium, 1995.

Once balanced, unstack the rotor . Place the shaft vertically again and this time stack the impellers together with the diffuser elements , in the same manner. After installation of every stage, check the float. A jack may be placed under the coupling end of the shaft; the required lift must be maintained throughout the assembly . Diffuser covers have a small interference fit of 0.01 mm and may require heat. If a cover does not fit, heat the preceding cover with a small torch around the entire circumference for a minute, then tap the cover lightly with a hammer. After all impellers and diffusers are installed, install the balance piston . Once cool, tighten the nut to the match marks made earlier. The impeller–diffuser line-up — the axial location of the rotor to give the correct gap — is adjusted by the thickness of the locator ring placed between the thrust collar and the shaft step .

The relation of shroud and hub positions to the diffuser/volute and casing must be verified and determined during assembly. Axially, the impeller discharge should be entirely within the axial width of the diffuser. If it is not, flow from the impeller discharges against the diffuser or casing walls. Rotor sensitivity to impeller and diffuser alignment depends on the ratio B₂/B₃ — impeller exit vane width to diffuser vane width — and must be judged case by case. A typical overlap of not less than half the impeller side-plate (shroud/cover) thickness is preferred. A balancing operation that destroys performance During dynamic balancing, if grinding of the impeller sidewall extends to the impeller OD such that it affects the overlap, pump performance will be affected. The balancing shop needs to know this constraint; it will not infer it.

Beyond axial location, two famous dimensions must be measured, recorded and corrected during overhaul. They have a pronounced impact on the hydraulic stability of any high-energy pump. Gap-A and Gap-B — definition and recommended values Gap Definition Range Preferred Gap-A Radial clearance between the outer diameters of the impeller side plates (hub/cover, shroud) and the inner diameter of the diffuser channel side plates . 35–85 mils . Beyond 125 mils it loses its effectiveness. 50 mils Gap-B (diffuser type) Radial clearance between the impeller vanes at their outer diameter and the diffuser or volute vane inner diameter , expressed as a percentage of the impeller vane diameter . 4–12% 6% Gap-B (volute type) As above. 6–12% 10% Where the number of impeller and diffuser vanes is even , the radial gap must be larger by 4% . The one correction that costs nothing and gains everything Correct gaps eliminate vane pass vibration frequency . And critically: machining the diffuser or volute vane to achieve the right Gap-B without affecting Gap-A causes no loss of efficiency. In fact, the high noise level, shock and vibration caused by vane pass frequency are eliminated — improving efficiency. This is why the data sheet should demand the impeller-to-cutwater clearance for pumps developing more than 200 mlc.

t: Inserting the inner assembly and final build
b: Insert the assembled inner subassembly — inner casing plus rotor — into the outer casing using a guide fixture . Install the expansion gaskets and spacers between inner casing and outer head. Improper inner head gasket spacers can result in improper makeup of the intermediate diffuser covers ; the suction spacer and discharge diffuser spacer could then allow liquid recirculation, dropping efficiency and causing erosion . Spacer thickness plus gasket should achieve approximately 0.4–0.5 mm compression on each gasket . Install and tighten the head. In most designs the head fit is all-metal and the gap at the head should be approximately 1–1.5 mm . Install the bearing housings with the lower half journal bearing in place . Move the coupling end housing until the suction impeller is centred in the wear rings within 0.025 mm — measurable with feeler gauges. Record the dial gauge readings of the seal housing bores and faces . Insert the locating spacer and the thrust collar. Install the seals before the bearings are placed in the housings. Insert the bearing housing dowels and bolt them. Finally install the journal and thrust bearings. The location of the thrust collar lines up the rotor axially to get the right gap between impeller and diffuser. Install the coupling halves and make ready for alignment.

Pump performance deteriorates over time, and it is always a debate whether to live with the problem or overhaul. Living with it means continuous loss of money through inefficient operation; overhauling means incurring the maintenance cost. The question is answerable arithmetically. The algorithm below is the work of Ray Beebe , from Condition Monitoring of Pumps can save Money (APMA Seminar).

Which assumption applies, and what follows Assumption Method Deterioration is constant over time A cash flow analysis establishes whether the investment in overhaul gives the required rate of return — the same process used for any plant improvement investment. Deterioration rate increases with time The optimum time for overhaul is when the accumulated cost of the increased power consumption equals the cost of the overhaul .

Deterioration limits plant throughput. The loss of production is high enough to justify the overhaul cost immediately — it becomes a matter of finding an opportune window. Pump operation is intermittent and does not affect throughput. Any deterioration simply means longer operating duration — typically pumps loading product into tankers. The additional operating time and excess power can be compared directly with the overhaul cost. Deterioration is initially offset by opening a control valve or increasing speed , but over time a threshold is reached and throughput begins to suffer. In some cases the power requirement exceeds the motor rating, causing overload trips. Use the performance calculation procedure to determine the power the pump consumes, benchmark it against the performance curves, and the difference gives the excess power consumption — which converts directly into lost expense. Pumps consuming excess power are the primary candidates and take higher priority.

Context 2 — the pump runs intermittently and loss of performance does not affect throughput. Given data Duration of pump operation 24 months, operating 27% of the time Cost of overhaul $50 000 Cost of power 10 c/kWh Excess power consumption 167 kW Assuming the excess power consumption rate increase is linear : Cost of deterioration at month 24 Hours in one month 30 × 24 = 720 h Hours of operation at 27% 720 × 0.27 = 194.4 h Excess power consumed in one month 167 × 194.4 = 32 464.8 kWh Cost of that excess power at 10 c/kWh 32 464.8 × 0.1 = $3 246.5 Rate of cost of deterioration, spread linearly over 24 months $3 246.5 ÷ 24 = $135.3 per month per month From there the process is iterative and easily solved on a spreadsheet. Honest limits of the method The calculation is only correct if wear progresses at a uniformly increasing rate with time. Information may not be available to make any other assumption, but decision makers have to start somewhere. Some relatively small pumps may never justify overhaul on energy savings alone — but may be justified on reduced plant production rate, where the deterioration does not affect production at least initially. Variable speed pumps deteriorate much more expensively For a pump whose speed is varied to meet its duty, the effect of wear on power required is much more dramatic than for a constant-speed throttle-controlled pump — because power increases in proportion to the speed ratio cubed . Unless the pump output is limited by reaching maximum speed or the driver's highest allowable power output, no production will be lost — so the deterioration is invisible in production terms. But power consumed increases far more dramatically for a given wear state than on a constant-speed pump. This is exactly where performance monitoring tools or portable instruments earn their cost, because nothing else will tell you. The same method and calculations then find the overhaul time for minimum total cost. Better expressed as a ratio scaled to suction energy. Cavitation Vapour bubbles forming where local pressure falls to vapour pressure, then imploding as pressure recovers. Damage appears on the leading face of the non-pressure side of the vanes as pockmarking and vane thinning. Incipient cavitation The actual onset of cavitation — at an NPSH 2 to 20 times the 3% NPSH-r. Causes minimal damage itself; the peak erosion rate sits between the 3% value and the incipient value. Recirculation Flow reversal at the inlet or outlet tips of the impeller vanes. Produces noise and vibration that imitate cavitation and is routinely misdiagnosed as it. Damages the opposite side of the vane. Cured by operating closer to BEP — not by adding suction head. Suction energy A qualitative measure rising with suction nozzle size, pump speed, suction specific speed and specific gravity. Low suction energy pumps tolerate thin margins; high suction energy pumps do n

Dimensionless and quasi-dimensionless indices Specific speed , N s N√Q / H 3/4 , with head per stage and no double-suction correction. Indexes impeller type, geometric similarity, attainable efficiency and curve shape. Conventionally in US units (gpm, ft, rpm). Suction specific speed , N ss N√Q / (NPSH-r) 3/4 , with Q halved for a double-suction impeller. The higher it is, the narrower the stable operating band. Preferred range 8 000–11 000. Head coefficient , ψ H / (u₂²/2g). Used with the flow coefficient to build universal characteristics that allow comparison between dissimilar machines — and testing on another fluid. Flow coefficient , φ Q / (u₂A), where A = πd₂²/4. L³/D⁴ The shaft slenderness proxy to which deflection is proportional. Widely quoted in bid comparisons and not a valid basis for comparing reliability between pumps — ask for actual deflection values instead. Modelling law Two geometrically similar pumps against the same head have similar flow conditions if speeds are inversely proportional to size; capacity then varies as the square of size. Used for very large hydroelectric pumps.

Components and configurations Impeller eye The inlet opening through which liquid enters the impeller. Single-suction has one; double-suction has two. Shroud The disc enclosing the impeller vanes. A closed impeller has front and back shrouds; semi-open omits the front; open designs reduce or omit the back shroud too. Scalloped impeller An open impeller with the back shroud partially ( partially scalloped ) or almost entirely ( fully scalloped ) removed to reduce axial thrust. Vortex / non-clog impeller A fully shrouded open impeller located above the volute that does not energise the liquid directly — it creates a vortex which does. Experiences almost no radial force, so it tolerates extended closed-discharge running. Recuperator Generic term for whatever converts impeller outlet velocity into pressure — vaneless guide ring, concentric casing, volute, vaned diffuser, diagonal or axial diffuser vanes. Volute The spiral casing collecting flow from the impeller. Single volutes are most efficient at BEP but carry high radial load away from it; double volutes reduce radial load across the range. Cutwater / volute tongue The dividing edge where the volute passage begins. Minimises recirculation and reduces radial load — and its clearance to the impeller sets vane pass vibration. Throat The narrowest section of a volute or diffuser passage, where kinetic energy begins converting to pr

Rotor behaviour and overhaul terms Axial thrust Net axial force from internal pressures on the exposed areas of the rotating element, plus a momentum term. Several governing variables are indeterminate, so calculated values are approximate. Radial load Force from non-uniform pressure distribution around the impeller. Near zero at BEP in a volute pump, maximum at shut-off — and reversed in sense in a concentric casing. Shaft deflection Bending under a constant unidirectional load. The deflected shaft rotates about its own bent centreline, reversing stress every revolution → fatigue. Limit at seal faces is 0.05 mm. Shaft whip A different motion: the shaft end orbits, generating a cone, with the centreline shifting 180° for every 180° of rotation. A rotordynamic problem, not a radial load problem — commonly confused with deflection. Vane pass frequency Number of impeller vanes × running speed. Excited by too small a gap between impeller OD and cutwater; corrected via Gap-B at no efficiency cost. Gap-A Radial clearance between impeller side plate ODs and the diffuser channel side plate IDs. Range 35–85 mils, preferred 50; ineffective beyond 125. Gap-B Radial clearance between impeller vane OD and diffuser or volute vane ID, as a percentage of impeller vane diameter. 4–12% (preferred 6%) for diffuser types, 6–12% (preferred 10%) for volutes; add 4% if both vane counts are even. b: The decision rule Service criticality decides the standard , not habit and not the engineer's comfort. Run the criticality assessment first. Selection guidance Service Standard Reasoning Critical refinery pump on hazardous hydrocarbons; no standby; high-energy duty API 610 The premium is justified by the consequences of failure and the cost of downtime. Ordinary chemical or general process duty ANSI/ASME B73.1 Ordinary applications do not need the full API feature set, and the premium is not justified. Dimensional interchangeability between brands is a real operational advantage for spares and replacement. Firewater NFPA 20 Purpose-written for the duty, including the flat-curve requirement that firewater headers need. Where an ISO basis is specified ISO 5199 + ISO 2858 5199 for design, 2858 for dimensions. 2858 alone fixes nothing about construction. Both failure modes cost money Over-specifying buys cost, lead time and spares complexity without buying reliability. Under-specifying a hazardous high-energy hydrocarbon duty to a general-purpose standard is a false economy that gets paid for in incidents and maintenance. Neither is the safe default.
